Hon. CHARLES MARC'IL (Bonaventure) presented the third report of the joint select standing committee on the printing of parliament as follows:
Your committee have considered the matter of salary of the superintendent of the distribution office of parliament, and are of the opinion that the salary paid to this official is not adequate in view of the responsibilities of the position and the increase in the work of this office.
Your committee have therefore passed the following resolution, and herewith submit the same for the approval of your honourable house:
Resolved:
That the joint select standing committee on the printing of parliament do recommend to both houses that the salary of Mr. R. B. Davidson, superintendent of the distribution office, be increased to $3,600 per annum, from March 31, 1928.

Mr. SPOTTON; Mr. Chairman, I have a question to ask the minister (Mr. Forke) which is directly connected with this vote. In August last a young man in mry constituency was given an appointment under the department of immigration; I think it had to do with the inspection of soldiers' farms. He comes from true blue Liberal stock and, so far as I know, will oontinue in the political fait-h of his people. The appointment was made one month before the by-election in ;North Huron, and the young man was promptly fired within a month or so afterwards. He left- a good position to enter the department. He was appointed, I believe, on the recommendation of Hon. Duncan Marshall. I have spoken to Mr. Marshall and to the Minister of Immigration, but have been unable to get any satisfaction. I have also tried to get another minister, who is related to the family of the young man, to intercede, but without avail. I have been told that this young man was not competent. I do not believe it, for no member of that family would undertake to do any work which he was not competent to discharge. I was shown some expense accounts of his which were not supposed to be well made up, but the only fault I could find was that his expenses were too low. I am confident that if the young man had been taken in hand by an officer of the department and given a white man's chance he would have made good from the training he has had as a member of an old pioneer family. He thought he had been engaged permanently; if the department engaged him for a short period before and after the byelection he certainly did not think so. I plead with the minister in the future not to allow his department to be thus used during elections. On behalf of one of my constituents-it is nothing to me politically-I wish to enter a protest against any mentber of the administration coming into my county and using such sharp practices upon my people.
I do not know anything about the facts of the case, Mr. Chairman, I will make inquiries of the chairman of the land settlement board.

Mr. Minister, if you do not know, you should because you were one

of the first men I called upon when I came here and I have been in touch with you continuously as well as with one of your colleagues in an attempt to have this young man reinstated.
(Mr. BSLING: I wish to ask the minister if within the last few weeks he has had a report concettming the Doulthobors in the West Kootenay district.
I have had no report beyond what the hon. member himself has told me.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee a very serious situation. In West Kootenay we have a rather large community of Doulc-hobore. During the past three weeks a fanatical faction, composed of about two hundred, have been on a rampage, marching through the adjoining municipalities, holding public meetings, chanting and speaking. No one objects so much to singing but their leaders are practising the worst kind of communism. They persist in standing on the street corners and openly defying the laws of the country. For instance, they declare that they will not send their children to school, that they will not register births, deaths and marriages, and that they will not pay taxes. [DOT]It is only within the past three weeks that this has happened. There are 200 of them to-day marching through the country, and to emphasize their determination not to abide by the laws of the land some of them-not all of these 200, but anywhere from half a dozen to a dozen-make public exhibitions by marching down the street absolutely nude. It is only within three weeks that the farmers' institutes in convention in West Kootenay voiced a protest to the provincial government. They said, "If the provincial government cannot enforce the law, for Heaven's sake, who will? Will the Dominion government do so?" I realize that the enforcement of the law and the responsibility for that enforcement is up to the province, but I submit that this federal government must share to some extent the responsibility for the behaviour of these radical fanatics. It was this government that dumped them into Canada. They not only brought them but bonused them for coming. It was about 1903 that $32,000 was handed out to the Doukhobors as a bonus for their having come to this country.
I ask the Minister of Immigration, I ask the government itself, to amend our immigration laws so as to provide for the immediate deportation of such of these fanatics as

Supply-Imviigration
openly violate the law by going around the country absolutely naked. Is that impossible? You may say that it is up to the provincial government to prevent these exhibitions, but there cannot be a provincial policeman in front of every Doukhobor, and the community covers a wide area. At this convention of farmers, one man entered a protest against these exhibitions. He said, "I and my family occupy ten acres of land. I have my orchard, and everything I have is invested therein. Across the provincial highway from my orchard there is a family, man, wife and children, of Doukhobors going around absolutely stark naked, and I have to submit to that humiliation and mortification " Such a condition Should not exist in Canada. I do not know what our relations are with Soviet Russia so far as deportation is concerned. Nevertheless this fact remains:	We
seem compelled to harbour these people, who to some extent are nothing more than human animals; they have no more sense of decency than human animals. We have paid them to come to the country; we have exempted them absolutely and unconditionally from military service; and we seem to be more concerned for their welfare than for the welfare of our own people. We seem, I say, compelled to keep them in the country with their open defiance and violation of the law; yet we are unable to retain our own Canadian citizens. The responsibility, so far as these fanatics are concerned, rests with the Dominion government and I ask that they take some steps to provide for the deportation of those who openly violate the law and express a determination so to do.
From this same community centre, where these farmers' institutes were in session last week, comes a letter stating that the rumour is strongly current there that it is the proposal of this government to bring into Canada 20,000 more of these Doukhobors and to place them in the Peace River country with a view to using them ultimately for railroad construction. I want to ask the minister whether that is so or not, and whether that rumour is well founded. Perhaps he will tell me whether there is any proposal to bring into Canada 20,000 or any number more of these Doukhobors and have them settle in the Peace River country?
None whatsoever.

Is it not a fact that
many of these Doukhobors were bom in Canada and therefore are not subject to deportation?

Some of them were born
in Canada. I do not question for a moment the right of these people to remain here after a residence of five years. But even so, anyone will admit that there must be some means of dealing with these radicals who offend every sense of decency. There must be some ground for the rumour regarding the entry of additional Doukhobors; because in 1912 an order in council was passed forbidding the further entry of Doukhobors into Canada, and we included along with them the Hut-terites and the Mennonites. In 1919 the ban was lifted against the Hutterites and the Mennonites but we continued to exclude the Doukhobors. But only last year, or in 1926, another order in council was passed admitting the Doukhobors, and that would seem to indicate at least that they have free entry to Canada under proper medical examination.
One question I want to ask the minister is this-and I think we are entitled to an answer:	Will he not take steps for the deportation, where possible, of such of these fanatics as "openly offend ev*ery sense of decency and not only mortify but embarrass and demoralize the local communities by their exhibitions?
Where recently arrived immigrants, be they Doukhobors or others, are unsatisfactory and do not obey the laws of the country, I think the department is prepared to deport them at any time.

But here we have a concrete case; it is not a case of "if" they violate the laws. I have told you, you have evidence of it in the newspapers out there; you have it from the provincial police there that this faction of fanatics is absolutely and openly violating the laws of the country. They are standing on the street corners preaching absolute defiance, saying "We do not propose to send our children to school; we will not register births or marriages; we will not pay taxes." And to this fanatical faction is attributable the fact that eight schools have been burned in British Columbia. They not only say what they will and will not do, but they emphasize it by open defiance.

The general
subject of immigration was dealt with sufficiently yesterday, and now we are justified in considering under this item the work of the department as a whole. I am sure the minister felt a little elated' yesterday when he was given a clean sheet, decoratedv
Supply-Immigration

and had medals pinned all over him and, as you might say, a garland of diamonds hung around his neck by the Prime Minister. Yet if we study the situation as we find it to-day there cannot be any gainsaying that we have some doubts as to the results obtained by the department under the minister's administration. It has been shown that we have lost millions of people, both by losing our own people and by losing those whom we have brought from other countries, and just here there is one point to which I would like to direct attention. During the years this government have been in power we have brought into Canada, according to the figures given by the government, some 573,000 people, but in that same period we have lost to the United States, including some few from Newfoundland the figures for which I could not get, About 591,000 people. In other words, we have lost to the United States more than the number of people we have legally brought to Canada from the old country at an expenditure of some $55,000,000. If that is a result from which the Prime Minister can derive any satisfaction I fail to see it.
The minister has admitted that the Ipolicies brought in by his department have failed, and it might be worth while .to take them up in order. In all these years the three-thousand-family scheme has only produced some 2,600 families, and if that is the best we can do with ministers such as the present Minister of Finance, the present Minister of the Interior, the present Minister of Immigration and his predecessor, there is something wanting. Then there was a great scheme by which we were to bring to Canada retired officers from India, men with money; that has absolutely fallen through. Then we had schemes to bring out Scottish people, and hon. members will recall the way the minister spoke when this question was discussed in the house one evening. I put on the order paper some time ago, a question in this regard, and the minister informs me that most of those people are still on the land. That is not true, and the government know that very few of these Soottish people have remained here; the unfortunate part of it is that a number of them have returned to the old country. We heard yesterday and last evening that it was a great thing to bring an immigrant to Canada and satisfy him, then send him back to his own country as an advertising agent. Under that scheme we brought excellent people from Scotland, placed them in parts of this country for which they were unsuited and, as we

prophesied at the time, they have returned to the old country dissatisfied. That is the sort of advertising we will get from them.
Then the Prime Minister said that this present minister possessed certain qualifications, and that we on this side of the house were dissatisfied with him because he had moved across to the other side. I do not know that we have any dissatisfaction with the minister because of that; he was more useful to us on this side because he had some criticisms to offer of the government then, while to-day his voice is absolutely silent with regard to the matters which he formerly criticized. Then it was said that he is an immigrant. I would like to know what blood is in any person in the country except old country blood; we are all descended from old country people. Then it was said that the minister had sympathy, but I would like to know where that sympathy can be found. He has driven away the parties who in past years have been the best immigration agencies for this country. He has fallen out with the Salvation Army and has absolutely destroyed their interest and enthusiasm in the settlement of this country. According to their own statement they have transferred their interest from Canada to Australia. The minister has fallen out also with the Anglican church. There was a meeting in Kingston some time ago at which it was said that the slogan of some parties in the old country was "Our trouble is not to get British settlers but to keep them out of Canada.'' For a long time that was disputed, but after a while the minister had to crawl down and admit' that there was some truth in this charge. This church has been one of the best agencies for the settlement of this country, but the minister has done his best to alienate them. The minister has frozen out the Bamardo boy movement. Whether that was good or bad it brought some boys here, and if it brought some bad boys it also brought some good ones. So I can hardly see that the minister has that qualification of sympathy which was ascribed to him last night.

The McConachie
case.

Yes; let us consider the McConachie case and try to find where his sympathy was then. The first question the minister will ask me is, "Well, are you in favour of bringing these mental defectives into the country?" I say I am not, but the minister is and has brought mental

Supply-Immigration
defectives into Canada, and I have details of a few cases taken from his own reports. One of them is the case of a mental defective whose condition is said to foe the result of eating tinned food in babyhood. When a medical department or some medical officer can put that over the minister certainly it shows a weakness. Then we have other cases here, to a few of which I would like to refer in order to show that the minister has transs-gressed the laws and regulations of his own department. Here is a case known as J. P., described as constitutional psychopathic inferiority, but given a permit by the minister. Here are two cases of infantilism; they are pretty close to this mongolian type, aged 17 and 14, and both given permits to enter this country. Here is another person described as feeble-minded and illiterate, but the minister issued a permit because there is a doubt as to whether this is a case of mental deficiency or whether the condition is due to lack of educational opportunity. Can you imagine anything more ridiculous? Here is another case, known as H. A., classed as neurasthenic and illiterate, subject to the delusion of being afflicted with various ills. Here is another one, 13 years old, incorrigible in school but allowed to stay in the country because the father is here. Here is another one, 18 years of age, psychopathic inferiority-emotional instability. These are all mental deficiency cases, admittedly so, yet the minister shows his sympathy by permitting them to come into this country.
Now let us consider the McConachie case. As I said before, I am not going to say that these people should be admitted indiscriminately, but when the minister admits grown up people and then refuses to admit a baby I want to say that it shows a want of common sense. By the admission of that McConachie baby he would have admitted also six excellent Canadian citizens. The medical officers say that in this type of infant not 9 per cent reach twenty to twenty-five years of age. It is not an institutional class. The baby has not one chance in a hundred to live, because the condition is a heart one, along with other things, and the first little illness that strikes the child will rob it of its life. It is interesting to know if the minister has shown sympathy, this great qualification of sympathy? No definite cause can be ascribed to the condition. It is not hereditary, but one of the conditions is due to a mother having her children too rapidly. Another condition, as shown by the medical authorities, is due to
some shock on the parents' side. This book by one of the latest authors says that certain of these cases have been found to be the children of soldiers who have gone through the experiences of the war. McConachie was a returned soldier. If there was any sympathy in the minister's make-up, would he issue permits to these grown-ups who could be restrained, and yet separate a baby from its mother? That is a type of cruelty this country cannot understand; it is an absolute want of sympathy. I have asked the minister if he would accept, as he has in many other cases, a bond from reliable people that this child would not be allowed to become a burden or a menace to this country, but I have had no answer from the minister. Under the laws of this country it is a crime for a mother to desert her child, and yet we can by regulations rob a mother of her child. If there was any possibility of a menace in this case, or the possibility of any liability being put upon us, I would say there was some reason in taking a little baby from its mother, but not in the case of a baby who has not got one chance in a hundred of reaching even twelve or fourteen years of age.
But the minister's appointment is not due to these qualificatios of sympathy and service. We all know that the minister was put in this office to fulfil and carry out what has been described as a morganatic alliance. You might say a marriage has been consummated although no pastor officiated. But there is a marriage, and we are told to-day that the union has not been a satisfactory one, and there are symptoms now of dissatisfaction in the household notwithstanding all the medals that have been pinned on him. In other words, Sarah has become old and is non-productive.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Very funny, isn't it?

The result is there is a loss of immigrants; there has been an increase of about eight hundred but it is not an actual increase. This department is the most important one in this country at the present time. I have no fault to find with the subs department, as both the deputy minister and Mr. Fraser have been very reasonable with the two cases I took to them in connection with immigration. I would say that that is where the sympathy lies, in the officials, but on the part of the minister there is an absolute lack of sympathy in meeting these cases.
I really think the department must get back to the sympathy and coordination with
Supply-Immigration

all cases which it had in the past. It is too bad if they have lost the interest and enthusiasm of such a body as the Salvation Army.
I have a little sympathy with what the member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) said yesterday. We cannot make this country attractive to immigrants if we only stick to one or two classes. We bring domestics out here and I know for a fact that a big majority of them stay only to complete their period in Canada and then they are off to the United States. This matter of getting British settlers here is a very important one, but we are not going to draw a great mass of settlers from Great Britain on an agricultural policy alone. Great Britain is becoming more industrial every day and the minute we adopt a policy which will make it possible for industries to be established in this country, we will have a flow of British settlers. They are there and they are ready to come. At present we have the handicap of seasonal employment. In the old days this Ottawa river was alive with men during the winter, as the lumbering business was there in all its ramifications. What has happened? It has gone, but we have the pulpwood industry, and if we had a proper pulpwood policy in this country to-day we would have all these mills on the Canadian side. Whenever you speak of interference with the movement of pulpwood to the United States, that great association known as the Pulp Wood Association is immediately on your trail and threatening all kinds of dire things. We are sending to the United States from eastern Ontario thousands and thousands of cords of pulpwood. For what purpose? Cross the border at a port like Kingston and you immediately see the big pulpwood factories near the town of Watertown. I would point out to the farmers of this country that when we send our natural resources out of the country we also send the best natural resource we have-the boys and girls. When our pulpwood goes over there to build up these mills the boys go over to obtain winter work, and they do not come back.
Does the hon. member know she percentage of pulpwood which is exported from Canada?

I cannot say, as I can only speak for my own locality. But if you go to British Columbia to-day you will find a movement of pulpwood from the coast, and not one stick of it is being taken away on Canadian boats. It is bought by the Ameri-
cans and taken away on American bottoms; it goes into American mills and gives employment to Americans, and our Canadian boys must suffer.
May I interrupt for a moment? My hon. friend is speaking of something he does not know.
I know what I am speaking about.

The law of British Columbia does not permit the exportation of pulpwood or logs except by order in council, and the only grades of pulpwood or logs taken out of British Columbia to the United States market are third! and fourth grade logs that cannot ibe sold) locally.
I want to tell the minister I have gone up the coast and I know what the law is.
I know more about it than the hon. member does.
The law is there but they are being exported.
Only the third and fourth grades.
We have stopped this exportation in Ontario, and what is the result? We are getting our factories and work for our own people.

In northern Ontario if the settlers did not have the United States market and had to depend upon the local industry, they would starve to dteath. They have to export and they do export their pulpwood.

This is not the only matter in which the hon. member is out of touch with his constituency. He has his mills up there to-day owing to the fact that the exportation of pulpwood has been stopped. That and nothing else has placed the mills in the Abitibi district and elsewhere in new Ontario in the position in which they are to-day. We could have ten mil's in this country, but they are at Watertown and other places in the United States. I am glad in any event that I have raised a little discussion on this subject. If the minister, much as I respect his good) nature and so on, will come with me sometime along the coast of British Columbia, I will show him what I saw going on there in what I consider one of the richest provinces of the Dominion.

Supply-Immigration
Three great pulp plants.
The point is that the United States mills are being built up on Canadian pulpwood and the supply is being drawn from British Columbia.
Not from British Columbia.
What is the percentage?

Never mind the percentage or anything else. There is the fact and you must face it. If the government and the minister would face it, he would find that he could draw from the British Isles today thousands of people whom he will not get.

Does the hon. member think he is fair to the committee when he gets up and makes a speech on the question of the export of pulpwood and does not give the committee the percentage of exportation that is taking place? The percentage last year was a little over ten per cent.
That is ten per cent too much.

There is a surplus production of pulpwood in northern Ontario which the local industries cannot absorb. Are the settlers going to destroy or burn that pulpwood, or are they going to be allowed to export it?

If the hon. member wants to know the percentage I am sorry I have not got it here; I have it upstairs in my room. He will be able to get it from the Bureau of Statistics. But in any event ten per cent of the pulpwood is a tremendous quantity of our natural resources going out of the country and there is no necessity for it to go out. There would not be a surplus or an excess if these mills were in Canada where they should be. These are our own natural resources.
Would the hon. member suggest that parliament should legislate where I shall sell the pulpwood off land I own myself?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I should point out that a discussion on the exportation of pulpwood is not relevant to the matter before the house.

It is absolutely relevant. One of the reasons that have been given for the decrease in immigration is the
lack of seasonal employment. What is the use of making any criticism if you cannot give something constructive? I am pointing out how we might get over the disadvantage that we have in connection with seasonal employment. One thing I was mentioning wa the possibility of building up winter employment in this country if we had our own mills and produced our own paper. The mere fact of the percentage has nothing to do with the matter. I am pointing out what we should do in order to keep more of our people at home, and this is quite relevant to the question of immigration. The Minister of Immigration has said that he has sympathy; that he gives service to his people. The production of commodities in our own country will be an evidence of sympathy and service. I have not by any means gone into the whole question, but I should like to close up the discussion with this summary. The minister's administration is marked not by sympathy but rather by a want of it. He has dissociated himself from those agencies which would provide immigration. He has now established a severe medical examination. I do not know that I would have any great fault with the severe examination; but if you make your examination such that common sense will not be used, then the absence of common sense in dealing with one intending immigrant will absolutely stop and debar hundreds from coming to this country and we will lose the sympathy and enthusiasm which we should have in the old country. Those Scottish people who came over here and were settled should have been placed where they would have been advertisements instead of being permitted to return home and say that they were dissatisfied with conditions in Canada.

speechtext: -carried weekly statements that there were irregularities within the Department of Immigration. In fact it was alleged that there was traffic in permits and the government promptly met that statement by giving the house a committee representative of all parties within the house. Hon. gentlemen named their own members of the committee. That committee was given a free hand to subpoena witnesses from wherever they believed they could get the information. The committee sat continuously throughout the session. They brought before them witnesses from all parts of Canada and they had before them officials of the department. Every opportunity was given to make good the charges that had been daily made against the Department of Immigration and what was the result? Yesterday we had presented to us a unanimous report. I am told-
No.
We did not have anything of the kind.

speechtext: Let me finish my sentence. I am told that some hon. gentlemen made reservations, mental reservations, as to what was in the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Just let us see that, right now. My hon. friend has charged that the Minister of Immigration of to-day has fallen out with tlhe Salvation Army. I am the minister that fell out with the Salvation Army. That trouble started when I was Minister of Immigration. And why? Because we had complaints from some of the boys brought in by the Salvation Army that the army was taking funds from them contrary to the understanding they had with them.. We sent for Commissioner Lamb. I was Minister of Immigration of that day, and I had an understanding with Commissioner Lamb. I pointed out to him the complaints that were coming in. from some of these boys. W!e did not have any quarrel with Commissioner Lamb. We recognized the great work that he was doing, but we wanted to demonstrate1 to these gentlemen that it was the government of Canada that was carrying on the affairs of this country, and was responsible to the citizens brought into this country, and that if he proposed to continue bringing these immigrante, all he had to do was to observe the regulations laid down by the Department of Immigration. I submit that it is not the government that quarrelled with the army, but it is the army that tried to work this up with the government, and they fell down on it, and I think they themselves recognize that they made a mistake. Why should my hon. friend blame the present Minister of Immigration for my sins? If any person acting on behalf of the Salvation Army has any quarrel, do not take it up with the present Minister of Immigration, because I am the man who is to blame.
I am sorry I have detained the house so long. I simply rose to say that having considered the- report of the immigration committee all day yesterday, a report which was unanimously adopted without anyone dividing the house, why should the business of the house be further delayed by attacks from here, there and the other part, of the house- attacks which I regard as a Tory attempt to work up public opinion against the Department of Immigration, simply continuing the attack that failed during the session and in the committee. Let us now get down to business and vote supply, and go on with the business of the country.

I desire to say to the
Minister of Finance that there will be no voting of supply if he continues to make speeches such as he has now made. I desire to say further to him that if he proposes to make inaccurate statements this house will not continue to vote supply. He said, as a minister of the crown, a few moments ago that there was an unanimous report adopted by the committee on immigration. Such was not the fact ,and it was stated here yesterday that such was not the fact. It is repeated here again to-day that such was not the fact. The minister knows it is not the fact, and he should not continue to make these observations. The Minister of Finance further stated a moment ago that this house unanimously adopted the report yesterday. He knows that it was carried on division, and was so stated. That indicated there were a number of members who did not agree with the report, but that the house did not vote upon it. He knows that is not a new custom. It was carried on by his own government, it was carried on when he was in opposition, and it will be carried on until the end of our parliamentary institutions. A vote was not taken in order to save time. But there will be votes taken before the conclusion of this session, if that is what the Minister of Finance wants. To-day or Saturday, whenever this

session ends, he will have votes on concurrence, on his supply bill. I assure him of that here and now. If that is what he wants, if it is what the Minister of Railways wants, they will both get it.
It is better than talk.
Three times the Minister of Finance used the word] "sniping." What is sniping? It is shooting from ambush or behind cover. The member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) was not sniping.
He is always responsible for it, though.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

No one in this house,
whether minister or private member, can charge the hon. member for Kingston with sniping. Such a charge is absolutely devoid of truth. The member for Kingston charged the Minister of Immigration with dereliction of duty, and gave particulars. Then the Minister of Finance said the merhber was sniping. Does he think it is- going to advance the business of this house to talk about sniping in connection with a charge that is frankly and openly made and that requires an answer, and to which an answer must be given by the head of the department, not by somebody else on his behalf. This capable minister, whose funeral oration was delivered last evening by the Prime Minister, cannot look to the Minister of Finance to make his defence. Every member is entitled to a reasonable answer with respect to supply. That is the sniping that is charged against the member for Kingston. I say it is unworthy of the Minister of Finance to make such a charge in view of what took place. That is not going to carry estimates in this house.

Well, we can stay here
as long as you can. There is no need to threaten.
We are not threatening.
Every word is a threat.

We are standing on our
constitutional rights, and they are not going to be taken away from us by the Minister of Finance trying to block supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Temperamental.
Not a bit.

Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has favoured me with a few very complimentary sentences since this debate began, and I am going to reply to him in exactly the same tone. I say that both from experience and temperamentally he is not suited to be the leader of a great party. I tell the hon. member that what he has said is very cheap stuff. If I have made mistakes, if I am unable to conduct the business of this department, I want him to tell me in specific terms what are my failures. He has made general statements about a broad vision; great schemes; millions of dollars might be lost; there might be failures-all these general statements he made and then recited them over again. That is the kind of stuff that has been handed out to this house and lauded as broadness of vision, as big ideas that will amount to something. What have I got from that side of the house this session? I came in at the beginning of the session as Minister of Immigration and Colonization, anxious and willing to listen to any suggestion that might be constructive, that might help me to carry on the department to the best advantage of Canada as a whole. At the close of this session, Mr. Chairman, I am without one constructive idea; I have not one thought that will help me in any way to carry on the department to better advantage. But I have got sneers-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Abuse.

Yes, and abuse; and I have been told that I am lacking in capacity and ability. I think if my hon. friend will go back to the province of Manitoba he will find that I have made a reputation in that province during the past forty years, that I have done something for the province. I wa-nit to say without egotism that I doubt if there is a man in Manitoba who has played so large a part in the public affaire of that province as I have during the last forty years. I am willing to leave it to the people who know me best, who have known me during" the years of my maturity, to deal with the cheap-sneers about my mentality, and about Sarah! I do not feel that my mental powers are less than they were, and I hope for long years to come to foe able to carry on public business. It seems to me it does not lend dignity to-the house to indulge in that sort of debate. I am willing to take all the blame for the mistakes I have made, but I think hon. members might at least have the decency to observe the amenities in speaking of a man's, private life or his capacity.

Supply-Immigration

Mr. Chairman, a good deal has been said to-day and yesterday concerning the report brought in by the agriculture committee and the statement has been made that it was not unanimous. I sat on the committee and the sub committee and helped to draft the report. There was one portion of it which did not meet with general agreement, and it was carried on division. I want to lay that part before the house. We divided on the advisability of taking up the transportation question with respect to immigrants from the old country, and it was decided that we should recomend the granting of cheap fares to those immigrants up to the teen ages; but when we came to the question of extending the same right to our own people, the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) objected. This was the section upon which we divided, and I wish to place it before the house. It appears on page 8 of the report:
The committee also recommends that measures be taken to ascertain whether the railways will restore the homeseekers' rates in effect prior to the war, making such rates effective eastbound as well as westbound.
In other words, we were to get in touch with the railways and see if we could get cheap rates for Canadians, because otherwise it seemed to us that they were discriminated against. For instance, a man living in Detroit can get 'a cheap rate to western Canada, but if he lives in Windsor he has to pay the full rate. We did not feel it was fair and square to treat Americans better than our own people, and we though we should get the same rate for Canadians who want to go west. That was the only thing on which we asked for a division.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to the clause referred to by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Donnelly), he has not correctly represented my abjections to that particular clause. He cannot be ignorant of the reasons I gave, for I not only gave them before the committee and the subcommittee, but in my remarks yesterday I stated very clearly my objection to including that clause in the agreement, or anything in the nature of that clause in the sulbamendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. C'ahan). I stated that a reduction of rates to move Canadians from one province to another was not a matter of immigration but of internal business of the country, and that while it was proper for a member to propose it in the house and get the judgment of the house thereon, it should not be taken up by us in the committee as a matter of immigra-56103-2504
tion. I believe I am absolutely logical in taking that ground. I do not think there is any use labouring that point further; I have stated my position on it. I am convinced that my own position is a logical one and if the hon. gentleman is inclined to differ from it, that is his privilege.

Was the hon. member for
Willow Bunch correct in saying that that was the only clause to which dissent was taken in the report?
Not exactly.
What other clause?

I rise to a point of order.
I think it is a well known rule in this house that proceedings in a committee, especially of a meeting which is held in camera, should not afterwards be discussed in this house; at least statements made in that committee should not be used in discussions in the house. I think that is a rule of this house; I ask whether that is correct. Hon. members in considering the matter should not refer, at least in detail, to discussions that took place in committee.

I have not
done so. I have referred directly to matters in the hands of every hon. member in the house, contained on page 8 of the report of the committee, and referred to in somewhat different language in the amendment proposed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George. I have not gone into details. I can go into details and give my reasons more extensively than I have done, but I have refrained from doing so. I do not see anything to be gained by labouring the point. I have stated my position, which I still believe is a logical one, and I allow others who differ from me to do so.
But I want to make a remark or two in regard to what has been said by the Minister of Finance about sniping. I should think that the Minister of Finance has been long enough a member of the House of Commons, and has had sufficient experience, to try out some new method whereby to have his own- way in this house, rather than to use the old threadbare methods which he has used for so many years. It is a very common practice of the Minister of Finance when he wants to get his estimates through, or the estimates of some other minister, or when he wants to block or prevent as far as possible any criticism of the government, to refer, just as he has done to-day, to the sniping methods of the opposition. I believe he was sitting in the house this morning when the hon. member

for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) brought to the attention of the Minister of Immigration as well as to that of the government a most shameful condition of affairs in his province. I sat here expecting that the Minister of Immigration would rise and give to that hon. gentleman some satisfaction as to what the government intended to do. But he did not do so. He sat there like a graven image. Not only did he sit there, but the Minister of Justice, the Minister of the Interior, the Prime Minister and these other ministers in the front row thought it was a matter of no concern at all. I presume that in the opinion of the Minister of Finance the information given by the hon. member for West Kootenay, to which he directed the attention of the department, is a species of sniping. We must not refer to anything of that kind because we are sniping, blocking the estimates. He must have included the references made by the hon. member for West Kootenay when he used the word "sniping". Could anything have happened in this house this morning which would justify to a greater extent any reference made to the inefficiency of the Immigration department, of the minister himself and of the government backing that minister, than the fact that what was brought to the attention of this house by the hon. member for West Kootenay was passed over by all the front row galaxy of notables and brilliant intellects of the cabinet?
Hear, hear.

Thanks for the ironical cheers. Just think for one moment of what was brought to the attention of the government by the hon. member for West Kootenay-a most disgraceful state of affairs in this country; and not a word of explanation. It was passed over by all this front line of brilliancy and not a word said in explanation. The hon. member for West Kootenay brought to the attention of this government a matter of very great importance and asked what the government were prepared to do, or what they would do along that line. He hinted or intimated to the government that deportation proceedings should be undertaken and he also hinted that the law should be changed, if necessary, in order to give the government the necessary power to send out of the country, no mattter how long they had been here, people who conduct themselves in the manner he indicated. It was not hearsay; the hon. gentleman, as in the case of the hon. member for Kingston, brought the facts to the attention of the department. And when we bring the facts to the attention of the department, we are told by the Minister

of Finance that we are blocking the business of the house; we are engaged in sniping, in calling attention to any deficiencies of the department and of the government. We can stay for the next six months-
So can we.

Yes, for
the next six months. The government have some of the qualities of the sponge: they can absorb all the bouquets and complimentary references to themselves, but you must not make criticism; otherwise in the opinion of the Minister of Finance, you are sniping the government. You must not do anything of that kind. "Hand us bouquets and we will cover ourselves with the flowers you send us; but don't offer criticism because you are blocking the estimates. You are being unfair to the poor Minister of Immigration if you offer criticism of his estimates".
The Minister of Immigration can stand it.

I do not
believe the Minister of Immigration takes that position himself. I should be surprised if any man of the Scotch race, to which he belongs, would take that position. The Minister of Immigration did not get up this morning and accuse hon. members of sniping at him because we offered criticism of his department; that remained for the Minister of Finance, following out his usual tactics in this house when he wants his own way. He has been long enough a member to try to work out some new method instead of using the old threadbare methods he has used for some time to a disgusting degree.

speechtext:
I want to
say a word with respect to the complaint registered by my hon. friend from West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) and stated again by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington. Surely both hon. gentlemen have been long enough in the house to know what the law is with respect to lawbreaking. My hon. friend made one statement that is hardly correct. When the direct question was asked by the hon. member for West Kootenay as to whether more Doukhobors would come in, the answer was given, No. With respect to the complaint regarding the conduct of these people in British Columbia, they are citizens of Canada. The Department of the Interior, my hon. friend knows full well, deport people when they are found to have committed any crime calling for deportation, and so recommended by local justices of the peace, when such persons have not been in the country five years.

The Department of Immigration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes; I mean Immigration. Surely that is well known; my hon. friend knows that full well.
I know it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Then why
the complaint that you are not receiving an answer? The situation is purely provincial; but if the individual has been in the country less than five years, in the event of any complaint, inquiries are made by the Department of Immigration and responsibility taken for his deportation.
I do not want to complain of the attitude of any individual of this house, nor do I wish to ward off criticism. Let us have it to the fullest extent; it is helpful. But as a minister in this government I do resent the constant reflections that are made upon the personal ability and mentality of members of the administration. I do resent that, and I want to say most emphatically but without any display of egotism that I think the members of the front row on this side will bear comparison with any member on the opposite side of the house. I have never refused to give an answer to any correct criticism, but I do resent very strongly being credited with not having sufficient mentality to size up any given subject with which I have to deal, and I know every other minister is in the same position. I yant to say to hon. members opposite that that is a favorite pastime of theirs, but. if they will couch their requests in parliamentary language I am sure they will always receive the most courteous treatment and replies from members on this side. May I plead, Mr. Chairman, that the decent amenities of the house receive some attention in that respect? Beyond that I have nothing to say; let us have reasonable and fair questions and they will receive courteous and decent answers.

Personally
I think the minister should welcome some reflections from this side of the house as to the wonderful mentality of hon. gentlemen opposite, if for no other reason than that a little difference of opinion might make hon. gentlemen opposite a little more humble. I want to ask the minister a question:	He
listened to the case presented by the hon. member for West Kootenay; the Minister of Immigration did not reply, and no one had anything to offer for him. There was hardly a word said.
The question relating to his department was answered by the minister.

The one
question of whether he was favourable to admitting more of these immigrants was answered, and he said he was not.

That was the question
affecting his department.

That was an afterthought. No reply was made by any member of the government to the matter of deportation, which was brought up by the hon. member for West Kootenay. Now I want to ask the Minister of the Interior this question:	In view of the representation
made by the hon. member for West Kootenay and in view of the disclosures he made this morning, does not the minister think some change should be made in our laws with regard to deportation which would enable the government of Canada to deal with cases such as that mentioned by the hon. member for West Kootenay even after the five year term has expired?

You must have a place
to send them.

I do not
care where you send them.

These people came here in
1903.

Hon. members will remember that in the debate yesterday we were told that we were not giving these foreigners a fair show because we were imposing our ideas upon them. For Gods sake let us impose some ideas upon people of that stamp, because the hon. member for West Kootenay is absolutely right. We should apologize to ordinary four-legged animals if we made any comparison as between them and those people to whom the hon. member especially referred. I say there is something wrong with our system of government if we have not the necessary machinery to put people of that class out of this country, even if they have been here for a longer period than five years.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will arrange for a domicile longer than five years he will find his question easily answered, but my hon. friend knows that if ahy individual residing in a province breaks the common law of the province, then the provincial authorities take control. That has happened with the Doukhobors previously: t.hev were arrested for travelling about naked

in British Columbia, and tihey were restrained in the province of Saskatchewan. All these things are unfortunate, but these people are citizens of our country and must be amenable to our common law. If that common law is not sufficiently strong to deal with cases of this kind then let us amend it, but when the answer is made to the direct question and the statement made that no more of these people will be admitted, the Department of Immigration has gone the full length in that respect. These people are here and they are citizens of this country.
Are they naturalized?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They have
been here for a greater period than five years.
But are they naturalized?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
So far as
I know many of them are naturalized. I am not aware whether or not these particular people under discussion are naturalized, but as a matter of fact my hon. friend knows very well that they cannot be deported to their own country after they have been here that length of time.
Yes they can, if they are not naturalized.
The great majority of these people came here in 1903;* they now have children twenty years of age who were bom in Canada.

Yes, but I was trying to ask the minister if he knows whether or not these people are naturalized. I must confess that I do not know; at one time my information was that they declined to become naturalized.
I think probably fourfifths would be non-community Doukhobors.

And that means that
they have reached that stage in their assimilation of our Canadian citizenship. The independent Doukhobor does apply for naturalization, and with respect to those people naturalization has been going on for years. As bo the proportion naturalized I am not able to say.

Is it correct to say that
the so-called fanatics, not using that word offensively at all, do not become naturalized? That was my information.

I think perhaps my hon. friend may be right with respect to that, but I remember that on a previous occasion I had reason to look into the matter of deportation, and of course immediately the question arose having regard to the changes which have taken place in the country from which they came. I do not believe that in the last few years we have succeeded in deportation proceedings with respect to people who came from that country a good many yearn ago, although they are not naturalized citizens of Canada. However, I really rose to speak in fairness to the great body of Doukhobors, because I know they are really assimilating Canadian citizenship; they are becoming good Canadian citizens and their children are attending the public schools. As far as the principles of their religion go,
I believe they would compare favourably with any others.

I should
think they would remain nationals of their own country until they became naturalized citizens of Canada.

I was very particular to
confine my request as to deportation, or as to some other means of controlling these people, to the radical fanatics. I made no reference at all to the community as a whole except to say that there was a very extensive community of industrious Doukhobors. My references were to the religious fanatics who to-day are offending the public by exhibitions

of absolute nakedness. In order to bring this right home, I would like to know what the Prime Minister would think if he went into his garden in the morning to pick some pansies or violets and was confronted by six naked Doukhobors.

I would send
for my hon. friends the leader of the opposition and the leader of the Progressive party.

There would be a riot
if you overlooked your own supporters.

You may treat this matter
with all the humour you wish, but I want to say that the home and the sanctity of his surroundings are just as dear to the settler in West Kootenay as they are to the Prime Minister. You might just as well say that your wives and children are to be offended by the exhibition of Doukhobors on these Ottawa driveways. These factions to whom I have referred are just a fraction of the community, but they are in the habit of going on these rs.mpages.
I do not want to be too pors,stent in bringing this matter to the attention of the Minister of Immigration, and perhaps I should address my remarks to the Minister of Justice or to the Prime Minister. I would ask them if the government will not take some means of controlling these fanatics who are offending the general public. Some of these people are naluralized, but not many of 'hem. and I know just as well as the Minister of the Interior knows that the province is responsible for the enforcement of the law. B ;* this government should share that responsibility, because they brought these people into the country under c.'tain coalitions, such as exempting them from military service. They not only brought them here but they bonused them to come here. We talk about undesirables being sent out of the country. Suiely this fanatical faction would come in that category, when they stand on the street corners and openly defy the laws of Canada. You can look at any of our local papers issued during the last three weeks and you will see the situation which now- exists. I ask the government if they will not take steps to remedy this situation. I do not say it should be by immediate deportation if the legality of such proceeding is questioned, but I would ask if the immigration laws could not be amended to provide for deportation or some other means of controlling this radical faction of Doukhobors who are offensive to everybody.
This is a serious matter, and I am not going to be shouted down. The people of West Kootenay want to know if this government is going to take any action to control these radical fanatics.

It has been said that a
great deal of time has been lost in discussing this problem, but I think the government brought it upon itself when the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) asked the Minister of Immigration certain questions. He proceeded to explain how these Doukhobors went around naked and so on, and it was the duty of the Minister of Justice or even the Prime Minister to get up and give the hon. member for West Kootenay some assurance that some drastic measures would be taken to stop the whole thing. There is no use of the government benches blaming our party for this discussion, because they are the ones to blame when they were not frank enough with the hon. member when he asked certain questions.

My hon. friend
from West Kootenay has brought up a matter which has been of interest to the people of British Columbia for many years. My hon. friend did not inform the house' that when Mr. McBride was Premier of British Columbia he had trouble with the Doukhobor settlement. He appointed Mr. Blackmore to examine into that colony, and if my hon. friend will read Mr. Blackmore's report he will find that it was not unfavourable to the Doukhobor settlement in West Kootenay. In addition to that there has been trouble over the burning of schoolhouses, but my hon. friend knows that the late Mr. Oliver, on a visit to Grand Forks, in the area where these so-called fanatics live, definitely stated to the Doukhobors that the laws of Canada would be enforced.
Did I not make my statement clear enough to the minister to convey to him the fact that these are the conditions existing to-day and not three or four years ago?

These conditions
existed many years ago, but Mr. Oliver stated in the presence of some hundreds of these people that the laws of the province and of the Dominion would be enforced.

But they are not being
enforced to-day.

The children from these colonies are going to school, and I think the government of British Columbia is effec-

I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said. Perhaps a word or two as to the origin of the Doukhobor sect and as to what they believe in might not be out of place at this time. The Doukhobors as they came to Canada were followers of Count Tolstoi. As most hon. members are aware, Tolstoi took Christ's teaching literally; he accepted literally and actually what Christ said, and he believed that it should be followed in a practical way not only on Sunday but in daily life. The result was the building up of a system or community which is referred to as Christian communism. They believe in non-resistance; they accept absolutely and literally the command "Thou shalt not kill". Some twenty-five years ago I had my first contact with this sect when I was shooting ducks on a slough in northern Saskatchewan. After I had been successful in bagging two or three ducks I heard a great deal of noise behind me and I found twenty or thirty husky Doukhobors with pitchforks in their hands racing down the hillside. They had left their farm-work and they were after me with righteous indignation because I had killed those ducks. I thought discretion was the better part of valour at that particular time and I got out of there as quickly as possible.
I have seen prairie chicken and wild game of various kinds feeding with domestic chicken in their yards in the villages, because those wild creatures very soon came to know that they were perfectly safe there. That was the basis of their belief. Under no circumstances would they touch meat. Under no circumstances would they drink intoxicating liquor or smoke tobacco. I have never seen anywhere in my life a better example of a really Christian community than I have seen in those Doukhobor villages. They were people of meticulously clean habits; they were moral to the extreme. Certainly they had some ideas to which we could not subscribe, but on the whole they were the very finest and best types of citizens and we never could find any fault with the Doukhobor communities.
Later on there came a stage where the communities started to break up and some of their young men were becoming Canadians. That is, they learned some of the habits of the Canadian boys, such as playing poker, drinking whisky and smoking tobacco. Some of them are quite Canadianized now. The

I hesitate to take any time
of the committee at this stage, but certainly during the debate things have been said to which I should like to refer and particularly the statement which has been made so often that the committee on agriculture and colonization were entirely unanimous in regard to the report. It is impossible to secure unanimity of opinion among forty members of the house on a matter such as immigration. I do not suppose there is any subject which comes before the house on which such a variety of opinion is held by members. The committee had to make a report to the house and the report which is made, I think, comes nearest to being something that could be passed by the committee. It is arrived at as a compromise amongst the different members of the committee. Many of us agreed to the passing of the report with several mental reservations. Speaking for myself, if I had had my way the committee would have reported against further assisted immigration of any kind, including assisted passages or free passages for boys, domestic servants or agricultural workers. My opinion is that the majority of the committee are in favour of largely cutting out assisted immigration, but this is not contained in the report and so I will not say anything further about it.
The attitude of the organized farmers in Canada will be found in the evidence of the committee. I am not going to read it here, but I will read just a few sentences from a letter which I have received from the secretary of the United Farmers of Saskatchewan. He writes:
We are opposed to the idea of the bringing in of immigrants purely for the purpose of settling up our vacant lands in order to provide revenue for transportation companies and pay an exorbitant toll to eastern industries.
I am opposed to the committee embarking upon any more colonization schemes. Our experience in the soldier land settlement scheme should convince us of the wisdom of leaving those things very much alone. Personally I should not like to see another dollar put into them. If we could forget about immigration and endeavour to make conditions right in this country, make them such that our people would find it advantageous to stay here, it would not be very long until our chief concern regarding immigration would be to have a very efficient medical inspection system which would keep out the undesirables.
I should like to remind the committee of some remarks I made last week in regard to the insufficient salaries which we are paying to men engaged in research and scientific work in Canada. Since I made those remarks I have received from a friend in Ontario a letter telling me about meeting in Washington a man who was at one time in the government service of this country. That gentleman is now engaged in the United States civil service at double the salary he was earning here. He said to this friend of mine:
Tell the people at home not to be crediting this country's progress so much to the immense amount of money it controls, but to the intelligence with which it is dealing with many of its problems.
I should like to take the opportunity of telling this to the people of Canada. If we would spend as much money on scientific agriculture and scientific research in many other lines as we spend on immigration, we would get much better results. The United States, which has received more immigration than any country we have any record of, at least in modern times, never spent one dollar on im-

migration propaganda. The only money it spends on immigration is for the examination of immigrants who come voluntarily. I should like to see in future this country lay the emphasis on quality rather than quantity. While I am on my feet I should like to suggest that the government, through the Department of Immigration, should be the sole agency for the issuing of propaganda and for the securing of immigrants who are brought to this country. I should like very briefly to bring to the attention of the committee the case of a family brought into Canada by the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society, a society which I believe is to receive a grant from the government this year. This man and his family were brought from some place in Ireland. They were, to use an expression which I have seen in the press, dumped off at Pincher Station, Alberta. The man was supposed to go to work for a farmer in that district but the farmer when communicated with said that he had agreed to take a hired man and not a man with seven children. This man and his family became a charge upon the community but following communication by the municipal authorities with the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society that organization have more or less cared for them. According to the statement of the society the family has already cost them $800. I am now advised by the rural municipality in that district that they have had to guarantee the doctor's bill, amounting to $62, and the funeral expenses amounting to $75 of this man's wife, who has unfortunately died since coming to this country. The man himself finally asked for deportation but the department would not agree to that. I think they have made a great mistake. Six out of seven of the children have been reported upon by the local doctors as being medically unfit and they are sooner or later going to become a charge upon somebody in that province. Somebody will have to be responsible for them. One child was in the hospital I think for two months. This may be an isolated case, but it is not the only one and cases like this should convince us of the wisdom of confining all immigration activities to our own department. If the department will take that attitude I will do anything I can to support them in that policy. I do not believe in granting money, to the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society, the Salvation

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of pleasure to the observations of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Forke) this morning. Had he taken the trouble to recall my remarks he would realize that I spoke in the very highest terms of his character, of his integrity and of his worth. I could not, had I been his warmest friend, have spoken in any higher terms of praise. But I conceive it to be the right of those who are in parliament, as it had been the right for centuries in England, to discuss the qualifications of any minister for a particular post. I took the trouble during recess to peruse the observations made in the British House of Commons with respect to a certain judge of the high court in connection with the discharge of his duties. I find that the present Lord Buokmaster spoke of the learned judge as having been guilty of folly and referred to his qualifications to discharge his duties. I find also that Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman dealt with the matter in much the same way. It would be a sorry day for this parliament if the great traditions and practice of the mother of parliaments to discuss the qualifications of ministers to discharge the duties of their office were no longer to be honoured by those who sit either to your right or your left, Mr. Chairman. Those who recall the language used by Lord Randolph Churchill in discussing so great a man as Mr. Gladstone are aware tha(; on more than one occasion he employed some very strong terms.

But even by Churchill's
friends his language was not generally considered to be creditable.

I am not referring tr
what he said on the hustings, but to the language he used in the House of Commons, language very much stronger than my criticism of the Minister of Immigration. I discussed-and as long as I have a seat in this house I propose to discuss-to the best of my ability what I conceived to be the fitness of the hon. minister to perform the duties of his office. If I am ever charged with ministerial responsibility I shall expect the same
measure of criticism from my opponents; I shall ask for no different treatment in that regard than that which I myself give. It is surely certain that a man eminent for his abilities in a certain walk of life may find himself in a public position for which he is entirely unfitted. For example, a man may be a great surgeon, but it does not follow that he is thereby fitted' to be a great home secretary; or he tnay be a very able lawyer and yet lacking the ability to become a great chancellor of the exchequer. His training, his environment, his attitude of mind)-all these things may wholly unfit him to hold a portfolio, and it is the duty of members of the House of Commons to be free and frank in their criticism of such a minister. My hon. friend was wholly opposed to the long traditions and history of parliament when he said that the members of this house have no right to discuss in any terms they please the aptitude of a minister to discharge the duties of his office. If an imbecile were placed in a position of trust as a minister of the crown every member would have the right to discuss and criticize the appointment. If some man, wholly unfitted in every possible way for the discharge of ministerial duties, is given a portfolio of which he knows nothing, we have a perfect right to discuss that, although he may be a most desirable citizen and a man of eminent attainments. While the minister we have discussed is a man of the highest character, a man of unquestioned integrity, a man who has made a very great contribution to the life of western Canada, it does not follow that he is fitted to discharge the high duties of the head of the Immigration department, or to give it that lead which is necessary for it to succeed. His complaint of a lack of suggestions from this house but accentuates our contention that leadership should come from the head of the department, and not be forced upon him by the members of the house, who, as they sit to your right, sir, support all the measures of the government, and who, as they are members of the opposition, support those measures which they deem desirable, and frankly criticize other measures which in their opinion are not in the public interest.
That is the position I desire to make clear, Mr. Chairman. I am very certain that if the hon. gentleman will be good enough to refer to Hansard he will observe that no better or higher tribute to his sterling worth, to his qualities of heart, to his high sense of duty, to his known integrity and character, could have been paid him than my tribute yester-

Who is responsible for the
newly arrived immigrant who becomes a public charge on the community?
There is no other provision but deportation.

But before deportation who
would be responsible?

The local authorities. As
reeve of a western municipality for twenty years I know all about that trouble.

Does the minister really
think that is a fair burden to impose on the municipality? In my view that is one of the things that in western Canada creates public opinion against further immigration. A few days ago I received a letter from a gentleman at Killam, in which he says:
I am writing to obtain a little information from you if it won't put you to too much trouble.
I am secretary of the local colonization board formed by the C.P.R. to look after the immigrants arriving and to find them work with the farmers.
Then he gives the name of a newly arrived Scotchman and continues:
He arrived here in April with very little money in his pocket, and engaged with a farmer. About ten days ago the man took sick with pneumonia and was brought to the local hospital for attention. He was in a delirious state and dangerously sick, and still is, his chief mental worry being that he had not the means to pay the expenses of the hospital and doctor. The doctor rang me up to ask who was responsible for this man's hospital bill. The farmer disclaimed responsibility, also the C.P.R. immigration department, and also the municipality.
A few days later another immigrant, from Czechoslovakia came into the hospital sick with pneumonia and with no money. Their expenses will probably amount to $200 and $100 respectively.
This amount, Mr. Chairman, is saddled on the hospital in that instance. While someone might have to bear the expense I do not think it should rest on the hospitals in these various communities. Under the present system the municipalities are not responsible for the care of immigrants until they are three months resident in the district, and some provision should be made whereby the party which brings immigrants into the country should be responsible up to that time anyhow.

I admit the hardship that is imposed on municipalities in cases of that kind. There is however, one aspect of the matter that might be taken into consideration. A great many of these immigrants add to the wealth and prosperity of the community, and that must be borne in mind. I admit at the same time that there is a hardship. This very morning I was discussing the problem with my deputy and wondering whether some scheme could not be devised to overcome such difficulties. I cannot exactly see daylight at the present time. Going back probably twenty-five or thirty years ago, I had a good deal to do with hospitals in the province of Manitoba, in Winnipeg particularly, where an effort was made to devise some method of financing, and I can well remember that this was one of the problems considered then. We do not yet seem to have solved it. I realize the difficulty, and if we can possibly find some way out we shall do so. We have discussed the question along the lines of boy immigration, wondering whether we could not adopt some method of the boys themselves paying into a fund and creating resources to take care of sickness and hospital treatment. I can assure my hon. friend that we will look into the matter with a view to finding some solution.

Should not some item,
say $2,000, be placed in the estimates to take care of immigrants who become destitute after having been brought in by the federal government?

Surely the organization that
brings immigrants in should bear some responsibility in the matter. The Canadian Pacific brings in people and throws them on the public, and in many cases they are saddled on the municipal hospitals. It is not fair.

That is along the line of
our discussion: we have been trying to see whether something cannot be done in that direction.

The hospitals are subsidized by the government and by the municipalities, and of course such losses will occur. I know that these problems are difficult to solve, but it must be borne in mind that all hospitals are subsidized to a certain extent both by the municipalities and by the government.

I have in mind a case
that came to my attention recently. A small hospital in a small town was run by a certain doctor. It received a grant from the provincial government for every patient therein treated. That grant amounts to 50 cents per day, whereas the hospital charges, bed and so forth, amount to $3.50 per day. I should think that after thirty years, as he says, some policy should be found by the department of the federal government to take care of a situation of that description. Can the minister give us an assurance that the matter will be dealt with? In my judgment it should be dealt with immediately; we should not wait for another thirty years to elapse.

I am afraid I am unable
offhand to offer any real solution for the problem. I do not think however that the hospitals incur very extensive losses in this regard. I admit that hardships occur occasionally, and perhaps the difficulty is greater in the case of smaller hospitals where the income is small, and where a large bill is incurred. But it is not a serious thing. I admit it is unjust; it is not right; and I can only promise that we will do the best we can to solve the problem. I have no solution to offer at the present time.

The medical men overseas are instructed under the Immigration Act to examine the physical and mental qualities of proposed immigrants to ascertain whether or not they are mentally and physically sound and to report. on agriculture and colonization the deputy minister stated that some 3,060 special permits were granted to members of parliament and others for the admission of immigrants to this country. My name was not on the list.
Hurrah.

I am not boasting about it; I applied for a permit but my request was not granted, and I claim that this was an instance where the good judgment of the minister could have been displayed. Stating the reasons by telegram and letter, I protested against the deportation of that child, and I still protest; I say the child should have been admitted to the country notwithstanding the regulations of the Department of Immigration, the Department of Health or any other department. McConaehie is a British subject; he fought for his country and was here for eighteen months before this happened, and he is justly entitled to that consideration which should be given any British subject or any Canadian citizen. I asked for a special permit to admit the child at least temporarily, and if the department saw fit to deport it later on, well and good. The family would have been perfectly satisfied with that. But she came as an immigrant, and the child also came as an immigrant, and, according to the Department of Justice, I had no power to do otherwise. The child automatically had to go back. I have been in communication with Mr. McConaehie and he has no heat in regard to this matter, and does

Mr. Currie called upon the

I hope it is true that the child is improving, but all the medical examinations we have had-I am no medical man and I can only take the findings of the medical officers-go to show that the child will not improve; I hope that will not be the case. I understand the child is to be left on the other side. Only the other day I read a statement by a gentleman from England who said that the child was returned simply because it was suffering from a cold. Some people say they are not afraid of a lie, but I am. It takes a long time to kill an untruth, and I have no doubt that this story has done considerable damage. The family has my sympathy. I hope Mr. McConachie and his little boys will become loyal Canadians and forget the trouble they have gome through during the last year.

It is not likely any boys
