On page 7 of the details,
there are grants to immigration and colonization societies amounting to $150,000. Would the minister give a statement showing how that money is distributed? It is included in item 56.

This amount is to cover
the cost of cooperating with the provincial governments in training schools for immigrants, and grants in connection with repatriation and colonization work. The provincial governments who have training centres get a grant of $10 for each boy training at their centres. The province of Ontario, the British Immigration Society in Montreal, and the Manitoba government, are all going into the scheme, for boys between the ages of fourteen and seventeen coming from Great Britain to go on the farm. This amount of $150,000 includes a grant of $50,000 to the Quebec government for repatriation purposes. I might say a few words in explanation of that.
For many years the Department of Immigration made grants to what was known as the repatriation fathers, priests in the province of Quebec who were engaged in the work of going over to the New England states and trying to bring back to this country Canadians who had gone there. Without entering into details, I may say that the department felt that we were not getting adequate returns for the money spent. During the Dominion-provincial conference, I discussed the whole
matter with Premier Taschereau, and he was agreeable to undertaking the work of repatriation if the Dominion government would make a grant on a fifty-fifty basis for the purpose. The provincial government in Quebec has been carrying on this work for some time with very satisfactory results, as anyone who listened to that paragraph about returning Canadians coming to Sherbrooke will readily realize. I think the money is being well spent, and that we are getting adequate returns. Under the arrangement the province of Quebec is to make regular returns to the Department of Immigration, showing the results of their activities.
This is an increased amount over what you were giving to the repatriation fathers, is it not?

It is a slight increase, but
I expect that we shall get a great deal more for our money in the way of results. It does not necessarily follow that all this money will be spent. If the province of Quebec spends $50,000 we will spend a like amount; if they spend $40,000, we will spend $40,000. and the continuance of the arrangement will depend upon the results that are obtained.

Is the government spending
any money on repatriation work generally, apart from this vote?

We have made the same
proposition to all the provinces. We will do the same for the province of Ontario, for instance. I think the province of New Brunswick has some idea of entering into this scheme and bringing back New Brunswickers. Nova Scotia is also considering it.

According to the figures in
the last report of the department, that for the year 1927, in the year 1924-25, 43,775 Canadian citizens returned from the United States to Canada; in 1925-26, 47,221; 1926-27, 56,957. This was the result apparently without the spending of any money by this government to bring these people back, whereas in connection with the repatriation work of the repatriation fathers, we have paid on on average in the last four years $36,000 a year, and their report shows that in 1924 they brought back only 333 people; 1925, 383; 1926, 829; 1927, 926, or a total of 2,511 in four years. Yet we are paying them on an average $36,000 a year. It seems to me that we are paying an excessive amount for the work these people are doing.

In regard to returning Canadians, we have a great many agencies at work other than the repatriation agency in Quebec. We have in the United States eighteen agencies that are engaged, not in repatriation work especially, but in the getting of immigrants, and of course as opportunity arises they will advise Canadians to return home. For the month of April, 3,000 Canadians returned to Canada, the largest in any month for a number of years.

My idea is that if this
amount of money was spent on immigration efforts in the United States, in getting settlers of any kind, instead of confining our efforts to repatriation work, we would get better results. If I remember rightly, we have only seventeen agencies in the United States, and according to the report, between 40,000 and 50,000 Canadians returned to this country. Whether that is due to the efforts of those agencies or not, I cannot say, but if it is, we are getting much better results for the money spent than from this other agency. Is the province of Quebec the only province that is taking advantage of this new arrangement the minister speaks of?

I would point out that the
province of Quebec is in somewhat different circumstances from the other provinces. We are spending about $3,000,000 on immigration, and very little of the new immigration goes into the province of Quebec. They are not getting perhaps their fair share of the money expended. They are anxious to get back some of their own people who have left the province, and have gone to the New England states in considerable numbers. With very little encouragement many of these people would come back. We shall not spend the $150,000 unless a like amount is spent by the provinces, and we shall not continue the arrangement unless we get adequate returns from the expenditure. It is an experiment, replacing something that has been in existence for twenty-five years, but of which there was a great deal of criticism. We are simply changing the system in order to do away with the criticism, and we believe that we are giving a fair and square deal to Quebec.

The minister says that
Quebec is not getting its fair share of the immigration coming to Canada, but I notice that on page 18 of the annual report of the department there is a table of immigration, via ocean ports, for the fiscal year 1926-27, showing occupation, month of arrival, and

destination, and it shows that the maritime provinces are getting the least immigration. Nova Scotia in that year got 1,702; New Brunswick, 911; Prince Edward Island, 125; Quebec, 13,735; Alberta, 11,780; Ontario, 34,000; Manitoba, 35,000; Saskatchewan, 16,000; British Columbia, 8,000. Quebec got more than the province of Alberta. According to these figures Quebec is certainly getting her fair share of the new immigration.

I do not think that is a
fair inference. If you will look at the figures for Manitoba, for instance, you will find that Manitoba gets more immigrants than Quebec and Saskatchewan combined, but that is simply because large numbers of the immigrants going out to the west go to Winnipeg as the distributing centre, and Manitoba is therefore credited with a great number of immigrants who have no intention of staying in that province. It is the same with Quebec. Quebec is the landing port for a great many immigrants who do not stay in that province, but Quebec gets credited with that number according to the table just quoted by my hon. friend.

Where would be the
landing place of the 34,000 who went to Ontario?
Different points in Ontario.
Where would they land in the first place, at what Canadian port?

My hon. friend from Camrose has been quoting from a statement of immigration by ocean ports. You cannot tell from that statement whether the immigrants stayed in any of these provinces. The chances are that those who were booked for Ontario points were going to Ontario, but it does not follow that those who landed in Quebec stayed in that province. It was their landing port.

It would seem from page
19 of the annual report, which gives a statement of immigration from the United States for the fiscal year 1926-27, that Quebec is getting her fair share. Quebec received 2,907; Ontario, 5,835; Manitoba, 1,290; Saskatchewan, 3,662; Alberta, 4,587. I want to make it plain that I am not objecting to the west getting immigration, but my point is that there has been a great deal of money spent for a certain purpose without getting much in the way of results.

I should like to congratulate the minister on the work he is carrying on in connection with the repatriation of

Supply-Immigration
Canadians from the United States. This work was originally taken up under the government of Sir John A. Macdonald, carried on all through Sir Wilfrid Laurier's regime, and is being continued to-day by the minister. As the minister very properly said, Quebec is one of the provinces of the Dominion which benefits very little from the new immigration. I have had the honour of representing a constituency in eastern Quebec for thirty years, and I do not know of a single immigrant who has come into that county since I have been its representative. The whole of our immigration is tending towards Ontario and the west. We do not object to that, but there is an intensive feeling in Quebec, and it has existed for thirty years, that we should keep up the work of asking Canadians in the United States to come back to Quebec. The Canadian returning to his native land is already prepared to carry on his work, and to become a good, and perhaps a better citizen.
There is another point in connection with this work upon which I am sorry the oom-mittee on immigration did not dwell very extensively. There has been an extensive campaign carried on in the province of Quebec in the last six months, petitions have been signed all through the parishes, and the French-Canadian press have carried on an enthusiastic campaign, in favour of inducing Frentih-Canadians to go to the west. When Sir George Cartier and Sir John A. Macdonald drafted the Manitoba constitution, their cry was then, Go west, young man. That was to stem the exodus to the United States away back in 1872. The only settlement of importance in western Canada at that time was the French-Canadia-n settlement on the banks of the Red river. The Manitoba constitution was made bilingual in the hope that a large surplus from the province of Quebec would follow the trails of t'he oourreurs des bois, La Verendrye, the adventurer, the explorer and discoverer of the old days. Long before the Canadian Pacific railway was ever dreamed of the men of Quebec went into the western country, following the lakes, rivers and portages, and settled that land. They shared in the honours with the Scotdh. The names of La Verendrye and Mackenzie wiil live forever in the history of the west.
Now, there is a feeling in the province of Quebec that if a man is leaving the province we should do everything possible to send him west, and the request that is now being made is that ample facilities should be given to the people of Quebec to go west rather than to the United States, and that to this end we should place them, if possible, on

the same footing as a Britisher or other immigrant from Europe. I know there is a difficulty in transferring the population of Canada from one province to another. That question was discussed many years ago, when Clifford Sifton, the greatest of our Immigration ministers, took up immigration in earnest and opened the great campaign which brought a thousand immigrants a day into western Canada for years and yearns, a movement which reached its climax in 1913. In Quebec we are anxious to keep our people, but if we cannot retain them within the province we should like to keep them in Canada. We try to inculcate in them the idea that Canada is not confined within the boundaries of Quebec, but extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Lately a new district has been opened up in Quebec along the line of the Transcontinental in the Abitibi region. That is but the beginning of a trek which will continue, and if t'he Minister of Immigration wishes to endear himself to the hearts of the people of Quebec, I hope he will! find means not only for bringing people to Canada but to retain those who are already here. Quebec is at the head of the Dominion in increase of population; it is the only province which has a birth rate to boast of. Its government is Betting an example in social and other legislation which is being followed in every other province. Our families are very numerous, in the rural parts there are from ten to twelve children in many families. The farms being small, and devolving to the eldest boy, the other boys have to go elsewhere, and if they cannot go to western Canada they pass over into the United States. Quebec is fast changing from an agricultural to an industrial province The development of our waterpowers north of the St. Lawrence and Ottawa river has transformed the position of affairs, and today Quebec is at the very pinnacle of its prosperity. It is the most prosperous province in the Dominion. If we cannot keep all our people at home, there should be a determined effort on our part to send them west. Those members from western Canada who know the French-Canadian settlers theTe will, I am sure, endorse every word I say. In the French-Canadian you will find no more law-abiding person, no more thoroughly British subject. Freneh-Camadians have stood by British institutions which they regard as their salvation, and for which they will, given the occasion, shed the last drop of their blood, as was said so truly fifty years ago by Sir Etienne Taohe, premier of Canada at the time of confederation.

I am endeavouring to impress upon the committee and upon the Minister ^ of Immigration the great importance of trying to discontinue the trek of our people to the United States by giving them inducements to go west.
I am told it costs about three or four times more now for a man to go from Montreal to western Canada than it does for an immigrant to come from Liverpool or other ports in Europe. This is a tremendous disadvantage. The French-Canadian press of Montreal, the pulpits and the agricultural societies throughout the province sincerely desire to keep our people within the borders of Quebec. If that is not possible we wish at least to keep them within Canada, and we believe by doing so we would render an invaluable service to this country, because the French-Canadian is the most typical of all Canadian types. He is a Canadian pure and simple; there is no other home country for him; his people's relations with France disappeared centuries ago and he would be as much a stranger in France today as a Frenchman from France would be a stranger in Canada. We go to France now and again, but we talk of things that happened three or four hundred years ago. The French-Canadian is rooted in this country, he grows up with it. He has always been loyal to this country, from the modest farmer to the statesman, and he has at all times rendered signal service in critical periods, and we all know to-day that the meteor flag of England flies from the summit of this building because of the action of French-Canadians in 1776- when there were few Britishers in this country
__and in 1812. We desire to remain British,
and we want to take our share in the work of developing western Canada. I know all parties in this house will agree with the distinguished leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in his appreciation of French-Canadians and the value of their influence throughout the Dominion. In his western home he has seen the oldest settlements established by French Canadians, settlements which are progressing to-day and from their colleges are turning out professional men who are taking their part in the public life of the country. I heard him say that the first time he pleaded a case in a western court was before the late Mr. Justice Rouleau, a relative of His Eminence, Cardinal Rouleau. We think we should offer every inducement to our people to go west and thus stop the exodus to the United States. French-Canadians have played a distinguished part across the line. A French-Canadian was governor of the state of Rhode Island, and there are so many of our people over there that they control the vote in many towns and cities, while several have dis-[Mr. Marcil.l
tinguished themselves by entrance to the local legislatures and the senate. But they belong to Canada. They wish to return to Canada, and if the present minister can do anything to assist them to return and go west he will render an invaluable service not only to Quebec but to the whole of Canada.

I quite agree with what the
hon. member has said with regard to the French-Canadian people being good settlers, but I cannot agree that it would be a sound policy for the government to pay any money to move people from one province to another.
I do not believe that is in any sense an immigration question.

We do not expect the
government to do that. All we ask is that relatively the same rates be given to the people of the province of Quebec going to western Canada as are given to immigrants coming from beyond the seas.

I objected to that clause in
the immigration report because I did not believe it to be sound. At the present day you will find in western Canada a number of men who went out there in the early days believing they were going to make a fortune in a very short time, but they have to work there just the same as anywhere else. There is no more free land, and many of those men have told me that if they could get back to Ontario or eastern Canada they would be very glad to do so. If you establish a low rate to the west there is just as good reason why you should establish a low rate to the east, for those who wish to return from the western provinces. This would result in our people transferring from one part of Canada to the other at the expense of the treasury, and I do not believe such a policy is sound. I wish to make it plain that I am not saying this in any way against the province of Quebec; I wish it to apply to all provinces.

I believe it is under
this item that assistance is given to immigration societies, and it is in regard to certain assistance given to an organization known as the Scottish Immigration Aid Society, operating in Alberta, that I wish to speak for a few moments. The question I wish to ask has reference to some property which this organization holds under lease. The minister will remember that some time ago I asked some questions on the point. In 1923 apparently they received a five-year lease at a nominal rate of $1 per annum for 1,100 acres of land with buildings, the conditions being that they should use these buildings and the farm as a distribution point and a training centre for

Supply-Immigration
settlers, particularly Hebrideans. I understand from the reply given that the lease was renewed in 1926 for another five years, from 1928 to 1933, on the same terms. I have had a good many complaints in the last two years from people in that vicinity as to the use made of that farm and the buildings-or rather the use not made of them; the farm has not been used at all as a training centre and distribution point but has been operated for profit by the association. I was informed that, during the last two years at least, at no time have there been more than perhaps five or six men on the place, just sufficient to farm it; and as it is good land within a few miles of a railway a good profit is made. I was sorry I could not verify this personally, as I usually do in such cases, for the reason that during the past two years my ability to get around has been somewhat curtailed. I have however, received many complaints from the ratepayers of the district to the effect that no taxes have been paid by the society; and when you remove 1,100 acres of taxable land from the municipality and school district, you increase the burden on the rest of the people. I understand the minister made some investigation after the question I asked and the information I gave him. I should like him to tell me the result of his investigation and what action if any he contemplates taking.
I was informed by the chairman of the land settlement board that the taxes had been paid on that farm.

A few weeks ago I
received from the secretary treasurer of the municipality and of the school districts duplicate receipts showing the taxes paid, and in six years taxes have been paid for one year, 1926. That was as far as they knew at that time, and that is only a few weeks ago. They sent the duplicates of the receipts. So far as they knew then certainly only one year's taxes had been paid.
Mr. FORKE; I do not think the farm has been a success. Only lately have the facts come under my consideration and I deemed it wise to advise that after a year's notice the agreement would be cancelled. Of course they will have to have the farm this year anyway. They may buy it and pay the price, otherwise the agreement will terminate.
Mr. SPEAKMAN; It is to the minister's credit that he took action as soon as the situation was evident. I am sorry I did not bring it to his attention earlier, but I was not in a position to go around my constituency during the last two years.
Mr. EVANS; I have always regarded immigration as the work of the government and the government alone. I do not believe in granting large sums of money to any society or organization, whether it be a business concern, a church or any other institution of that kind. We have been giving large sums of money in the past for this purpose, and so far as results go it has been a failure. We can look back now and say that the west has been colonized in a most successful manner, but that has been due practically to the richness of the soil and to free lands. These are no longer to be had, and immigration should be directed to a very careful manner, whatever way we go about it. I do not believe at present in allowing any business or religious concern to direct waves of humanity which too often are only exploited.
Not many years ago I was in Alberta when the Canadian Pacific Railway conceived the idea of partly equipping farms for settlers.
I was in Sedgewick about the beginning of that period when they landed some very fine live stock at that point. These were being branded while I was there. The official brand was made in large letters on the side of the animal and underneath three other large letters, "C.P.R.," were branded]. I asked the director the reason for this. I wanted to know why they should torture the animal to such an extent by putting these large letters on its side. I asked, "Why put C.P.R. at all? Would not the official brand do?" The answer was, "How should we know our stock when we came to make seizures in the fall?" I want to direct the attention of the committee to the seriousness of immigration work and its failure since 1911 particularly. I have the official figures under my hand. But let me for a moment return to the granting of sums of money to certain bodies. A great bitterness was engendered throughout the country last year through the circulation of an order for return showing that under the Roman Catholic Church some twenty-nine priests were in the work of immigration and repatriation, not all of them drawing salaries but most of them getting expenses. The salaries were not large, but why should this be done at all? This is the work of government. If any church wants to do it, let it. But the point I make is this-and I wish my Roman Catholic friends to understand that I have no prejudice at all against them: the method we are adopting is dividing our people, making clearcut lines throughout western Canada. I do not care very much from what country you bring immigrants if you will let them settle among others and not make any
Supply-Immigration

clearcut line. Do not make western Canada a replica of the Balkan states. I have no doubt that if this plan is carried on extensively something of the same results will be experienced in this country as in southern Europe. So much for that.
I stated that immigration had been practically a failure. The last official figures I have are from the Bureau of Statistics over the signature of Mr. Coats. I find that in the census period between 1911 and 1921-the period practically of which I have been speaking-we lost 19,958 farmers from the land. That is a loss from Canada of almost 20,000 farmers during that census period. Prom the province of Ontario, where we are told there is a home market and for which we have sacrificed agriculture in order to build up the cities, I find that we lost 33,722 farmers, and I think this is an appalling figure especially when we are considering spending such large sums of money to gather up people from other parts of the world to occupy our vacant land. I find that Quebec lost 13,165 farmers, New Brunswick lost 3,181, Nova Scotia lost 4,623 and the little province of Prince Edward Island, the garden of Canada, lost 3,159 farmers.
There is a cause for all this, and I should like to impress upon this house that agriculture cannot stand any more burdens for the sake of any other industry. Yesterday the Minister of Railways made the statement that an immigrant coming to this country and expecting the government to do a great deal for him invited failure from the beginning, and I want to tell the house that we have had a real object lesson in that regard. Our urban industries have failed, after all we have sacrificed to build them up, for the simple reason that before an industry will open its doors in this country it must link up with the politicians.
I have dealt with five of the eastern provinces; let me give the figures for the western provinces, and we must remember that during 1911, 1912 and 1913 particularly we engaged in the work of immigration very vigorously. During that ten year period the number of farmers in Manitoba increased by 16,931; those in Saskatchewan increased by 14,260, in Alberta 'by 17,376 and in British Columbia by 8,527. I think these figures must be startling to the people of this country; in spite of the great effort we have made to people our vacant lands to-day we have 20,000 farmers less than we had in 1911. Surely there is a reason for this, and I want to say that if we only keep our people on the farms our country will go ahead much more quickly than is the case at present.- We have not only 
brought agriculture to a precarious position but -we have even destroyed the purchasing power which is needed by our industries in the urban centres. So I say, Mr. Chairman, that before we spend such large sums of money we should consider this business very seriously and we should consider the purpose for which we should bring in immigrants.
During a great part of every year we have to face a tremendous unemployment problem. I have read some of the immigration literature which is sent throughout the British Isles, which states that if a man is willing to work and to put his shoulder to the wheel he is sure to make a success in Canada. I want to inform this country that the time has come when there are no wheels to which he can put his shoulder; we have sacrificed agriculture in order to build up these industries and they have failed to do that which they were expected to do, as the hon. member for East Calgary said yesterday; they have failed to provide employment for the working men. So we are continually losing these men to the republic to the south.
I have very little more to say, Mr. Chairman, but I think this is one of the most serious problems facing Canada to-day. We must entirely alter our fiscal policy, because it is wrong, and let me impress upon hon. gentlemen that the industry of agriculture surely needs to be as well treated as any other industry. However, I want to say that the farmers of this country do not need protection now; in the main they are not asking for protection but they are asking to be relieved of the burden of all the other industries, which they have been carrying in the past.

After listening to the last speaker and to the remarks of hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) I have been asking myself seriously if there is not a lot of insincerity in the remarks we hear from hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to the exodus of Canadian farmers to the United States. Last night the leader of the opposition said it was a pity to see so many thousands of young Canadian farmers leaving their farms to go to the United States; that it was alarming, and that something should be done to keep those young farmers in Canada. Yet when we come to this house or to the agricultural committee and propose some scheme for the purpose of keeping Canadians on the farms of Canada we are met by the opposition of our friends across the way, who tell us that this is not a question of immigration. Of course it is not; we agree

Supply-Immigration
on that, but it certainly is a question of prevention-we should prevent the emigration of Canadians to the United States. It is also a matter of colonization, and I think if we could devise some means of keeping young Canadians in this country on the farms we would be doing well. So it seems to me that before we bring in a lot of immigrants at the expense of the country we should do something to keep the people we already have. It is true that many farmers leave the land in eastern Canada; the hon. member who just took his seat gave the figures for the different provinces, and our first duty is to devise ways and means of keeping these men on the farm.
We have advocated in this house that we should give these farmers the same advantages we give the immigrants we bring from other countries. If we are going to assist immigrants to come to Canada we should give the same measure of assistance by way of assisted transportation to our own young people. It was demonstrated in the committee on agriculture and colonization that the difficulty in increasing the population of Canada is one of transportation, and that is why the committee recommended that aid be given by way of assisted passages. We advocate that the same measure of assisted transportation should be given to our Canadians, and we claim that if it were, the farmers in the east would remain in Canada instead of going to the United States. Transportation has a lot to do with that exodus or migration from Canada. Distances are great in Canada; transportation is very costly, and instead of our people going to western Canada on to the millions of acres of vacant land within twenty miles of the railroad, of which the leader of the opposition spoke last night, they are going to the nearer cities of the United States to earn their living. If it is considered proper to subsidize the steamship companies; if it is considered right to pay the passages of young boys between the ages of fourteen and nineteen years to come from England to Canada, it seems to me that it should be right and proper to pay part of the transportation expenses of young Canadian farmers in order to prevent their going to the United States and enable them to establish themselves on these millions of acres of vacant land within twenty miles of the railroad. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that we will got into trouble through the action of this government in connection with assisting immigrants to come here to take the place of Canadian farmers who leave us. It seems to me that we will be called upon to give an explanation to our constituents of the recommendations made in the report of the
committee with regard to further extending the facilities to enable people to come here at the expense of this country. Our farmers will ask us why they are called upon to pay taxes when they cannot themselves get any assistance to modernize their ways of farming, and to raise the level of agriculture in their section of the country. They will want to know why we are paying out such large sum" of money to give free rides to strangers wb come to Canada to take the place of ou" farmers who have left through lack of assistance. When the fanners of eastern Canada are tired of paying taxes to give free rides to everybody, probably the government will give us a Duncan commission to find out what we are mad about.

It is not then to be wondered at that the people of that province are watching eagerly the fate of the two bills that have been presented to this house, the Bell Telephone bill and the bill to safeguard the people s interests, moved by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary).
The Bell Telephone Company has been operating in Canada since 1880 and it is only since 1909 or 1910 that the company has become subject to the jurisdiction and authority of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Since that has been true the Bell Telephone Company has been most generously treated by the Board of Railway Commissioners and by the people of Ontario and Quebec. In 1919 it was permitted to make a flat increase of 10 per cent and in 1921 of 12 per cent; and a few months ago another increase was allowed, the disposal of the profits of which is now causing the company concern and in all prob-
ability is the reason for the bill which is now before the house. The raise in rates was allowed on the principle:
That non-diseriminatory rates should be established by the company sufficient to produce revenue to cover its operating expenses; a proper amount for depreciation and amortization; its taxes, including income tax, interest, dividends upon its stock and a reasonable surplus.
The Globe in an editorial on May 23, 1928, has this to say:
A dividend rate of 8 per cent is maintained, and the board has accepted the estimated requirements of the company for depreciation, with one small exception. There are few corporations in the country but would welcome a guarantee of solvency and earnings such as the Bell company obtains.
All this is paid for by the telephone users. In justice to these, should should not the board be authorized to make certain that the revenues of the company are devoted to the company's business exclusively ?
In the mind of anyone who has looked closely at this matter there is the suspicion that a close relationship exists between the Northern Electric Company and the Bell Telephone Company, amd that in all probability the Bell Telephone Company has used the Northern Electric Company bo conceal its profits. At least it is true that the Northern Electric Company is controlled by the Bell Telephone Company, and in the year 1926 the Bell Telephone Company was a customer of the Northern Electric Company to the extent of 5/.8 per cent of its total business. In 1926, according to Mr. R. A. Reid, barrister, who was counsel for the Ontario government at the last 'hearing before the Board of Railway Commissioners and also at the appeal from that hearing before the cabinet, $12,000,000 of apparatus, supplies and equipment were sold by the Northern Electric Company to the Bell Telephone Company, and at the end of that year the Northern Electric: Company had total reserves and surplus amounting to $8,400,070, with property and plant valued at $9,882,053. For the years from 1920 to 1925 the depreciation reserve ranged from 100 per cent to 129 per cent; that is what was set aside yearly for depreciation of plant and equipment. Surely this is a satisfactory financial condition, yet the Bell Telephone Company, which owns 52 par cent of the stock of the Northern Electric Company, does not show any share in its profits. They would rather receive their profits through an increased rate granted by the Board of Railway Commissioners, which is levelled on the people of Ontario and Quebec. Under the statute as it is at present, the Board of Railway Commissioners cannot investigate the Northern

Electric Company, and it seems quite clear that the right to investigate the subsidiaries of the Bell Telephone Company, among them the Northern Electric Company, should be granted by parliament to the Board of Railway Commissioners. If we, as a parliament, do not grant the Board of Railway Commissioners the right and power to investigate the subsidiary companies of the Bell Telephone Company, surely we cannot be said to be safeguarding the interests of the people. The Geary bill, which has not come up for consideration, was designed to do that very thing.

We have 245 members in this chamber who have openly, eloquently and solemnly promised at election times to work very hard in the interests of the public and to do w'hat they could to safeguard the common people against attack from any source whatever. This is a fine opportunity to make good that promise. Undoubtedly the members of this house, by defeating the Bell Telephone bill as it stands at present, have an opportunity to serve the people in Ontario and Quebec, and indeed- the people of all Canada.
One would hesitate to say that a Liberal government is more interested in a bill which proposes to increase the capital of the Bell Telephone Company from 175,000,000 to $150,000,000 than in safeguarding the people by passing with that bill an amendment which will make it possible to have the affairs of the subsidiary companies investigated when the Bell Telephone Company comes before the Board of Railway Commissioners to ask for an increase in rates, or by adopting the Geary bill, which will do the same thing. I think there is no doubt that at some future date the Bell Telephone Company will again appear before the Board of Railway Commissioners asking for a guarantee of dividends on their increased capital, should this bill pass. If it weire true, as we hope it is not, that the predominant element within a Liberal government stands for that principle of looking after special privilege
before looking after the interests of the masses of the people, one might well ask if that is a good Liberal principle or doctrine.
The thing which makes the Bell Telephone Company bill look suspicious is this: If there is to be no milking of profits from the Bell Telephone Company by the Northern Electric Company why should not the Bell Telephone Company welcome a full and free investigation into the affairs of the Northern Electric Company and its other subsidiaries? Some friends of the bill claim that the company wants more capital with which to extend its business. If that is true, why did not the friends of the bill support the Garland amendment in this house, which to me seemed the easiest and most sensible course to adopt if an increase in capital were desired, since it provided for the sale of stock in the open market. The house defeated that amendment; and from that we can only conclude that the amendment was defeated by the friends of the Bell Telephone Company, which leads us to be exceedingly suspicious of the reason for this doubling of capital. I think the Globe of Monday, May 28, 1928, makes it very clear when it says, in a short editorial on the first page of the second section:
Why-if everything is straightforward, clean-cut and aboveboard-does not the Bell Telephone corporation welcome the Geary bill, which would effectively establish its bona tides.
Why-if everything is straightforward, clean-cut and aboveboard-does not the Bell Telephone corporation welcome the proposal to offer this new stock to the public at the market price, which would effectively dispose of any suspicion that the public service monopoly plans to "cut a melon" among its privileged shareholders, as was done the other day by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company?
One of the chief reasons given by the Bell Telephone Company for the increase requested when they last appeared before the Board of Railway Commissioners was that they needed the increase to enable them to pay dividends on their stock. Now they want to double the amount of that stock, and I suppose the next step would be to go back to the Board of Railway Commissioners and ask for increased rates in order to guarantee an 8 per cent dividend on the increased capitalization. Again, that will result in swollen profits with which they will have to do something, and if they take the same step again they will increase their capital and then go back to the Board of Railway Commissioners and have their rates raised sufficiently high to enable them to pay dividends on the increased capital; that will go on endlessly.

He thinks he is, that is all.

-the connection between the high rates paid by our people and the profits of all these other companies cannot fail to be noticed. This milking process has now been going on for some time. The Bell Telephone Company has been successful in hiding from the people who pay the rates the amount of their profits. Some they have hidden in depreciation much greater than they use, as I will show in a moment, and some they have hidden in the Northern Electric Company.
The depreciation set aside by the Bell Telephone Company has been hiding enormous profits in the past. I am now quoting from page 15 of the petition in appeal:
From the year 1912 down to the year 1920, it has taken out of the telephone users and subscribers of Ontario and Quebec, under the guise or mark of a depreciation charge, the sum of over $39,000,000, and has only used or spent out of that money for the purpose of depreciation for which it "was extracted from the telephone users, the sum of about $13,000,000, leaving a sum of over $26,000,000, taken out of the pockets of the said telephone users of Ontario and Quebec in extortionate, high and excess telephone rates during that period of time, and which will never be spent for the express specific purpose for which it was squeezed out of the said telephone users, and is still being added to and piled up at the rate of over $1,500,000.

That would seem to show that the Bell Telephone Company is hiding what is really profit under the name of depreciation.
When we consider the way they have of dealing with the income tax, we find that they keep the public from knowing just how much they are making out of the rates charged. On page 11 of this same petition in appeal we find the following:
The question of income tax was not properly dealt with by the railway commission, and no definite finding, judgment, or decision was arrived at, thus leaving in the air an item of over $400,000, which your petitioners contend should not be allowed at all as an operating expense of the company, as has been done, but should be deducted from the company's net earnings and paid by the company and its shareholders, and not by the subscribers and telephone users, nor shifted by the company in such a way as to have to be paid by the telephone users; nor is the company entitled to, by rate increases or otherwise, sufficiently high rates to meet the payment of such income tax payment. It must be paid by the company direct as an entity or person out of and from surplus and net profits. It is not an operating expense.
Mr. Reid goes on to show that the method used by the Bell Telephone Company in the paying of their income tax is contrary to the statute under which the income tax branch of the Department of National Revenue operates, and he quotes as follows:
It is under and by virtue of section 3, subsection 8, of 13 and 14 George V. chapter 52. statutes for 1923. that the department acts, and that is the authority under which an item of this kind, put in as an operating expense, is disallowed as such.
And further on:
The application of the Bell Telephone Company for an increase of rates was based upon the operations for the year 1925, and the company showed a nominal paper bookkeeping deficit of $8,712 for that year. But it improperly charged its income tax payment, amounting to $320,000, as an operating expense. If this had not been done, and had the income tax payment been dealt with in a proper manner as hereinbefore explained, there would have been a surplus of over $300,000 in 1925, instead of a deficit, and the application of the company should have been dismissed.
And then, to my mind, he clinches the matter in the last three lines on page 12 by saying:
The Bell Telephone Company should stand in no more favourable position than the wage earner, or the salaried individual, who must pay his income tax out of his net earnings.
The Bell Telephone Company have been doing very nicely for themselves by passing their income tax on down and charging it to the telephone users in higher rates. Added to that, they have been sinking very large sums of money in depreciation reserves that

have never been used for that purpose. It would seem to me that the members of this house, who represent after all, if they are guided by their professions, the telephone users rather than the Bell Telephone Company, should take such steps as will prevent the Bell Telephone Company on the one hand, from hiding its profits, and on the other, from passing its income tax on down to the people on the ground floor. When we think of anyone, no matter where he lives or what his job is, who has a telephone, he pays not only his own income tax but a share of the income tax of this wealthy Bell Telephone Company of Canada and its subsidiary companies. Surely that is not fair. If people pay their own income tax that should be enough without asking them to pay the other fellow's as well.
As I am a representative of a constituency which is almost wholly agricultural, I think it would be well to consider the position of the farmer in regard to the increased rates, and in regard to the income tax which is passed on down. There are many people besides the Bell Telephone Company who are in the position of passing their increased cost of living and their income tax on down the line until it reaches the place where it can be passed no farther, and that fellow must pay up. In this case that fellow is the farmer. The farmer in Ontario or Quebec who uses a telephone and indeed, whether he uses it or not, pays for the increased telephone rates of many people. He pays it not only for himself but also for the increased rates of the telephone that his doctor uses, the increased rates of the telephones used by his dentist, by the merchant from whom he buys his supplies, by the minister whom he hears preach on Sundays. He pays for the increased rates of the telephones used by the implement agent, the man who runs the gasoline station, the blacksmith who shoes his horses, the editors of the newspapers, both daily and weekly, that he reads. Indeed he pays the increased telephone rate of the dealer to whom he sells his farm products, if he has not yet developed intelligence enough to know that he should sell his own products in cooperation with his fellows. Last, but certainly not least, he pays the increased telephone charges of the undertaker, or at least his estate does. The farmer is on the ground floor. He cannot pass his increased costs of living due to the rates on to somebody else. I have heard a great deal in the house about the farmer not paying an income tax. Hon. members now know the reason. He is so busy paying other people's he has not anything left to pay his own. It is not any wonder at all that the agriculturists are getting out from under the load.
In conclusion, if the government care for the people, indeed, if they care only for themselves and wish to maintain themselves in the position which they now happily occupy-
I mean happily for them-it would be very well for them to do everything in their power to ditch the Bell Telephone bill as it is at present constituted. If by the Sanderson amendment it is as well safeguarded as it would be by the Geary bill-and I am not in a position to say whether it is or not- it would put the matter in a different light; but the Bell Telephone bill should be safeguarded in such a way that the people of Ontario and Quebec will not again be forced to pay higher rates which will enable the Bell Telephone Company to pay dividends on its increased capitalization.

That, is the view that I take in regard to the matter, and if those who are sponsoring in parliament the bill of the Bell Telephone Company have confidence in the merits of their case and in the request of that company for an increased capitalization, they can well afford to wait until all classes of the people-because practically all the people of Canada are interested in this matter-have had an opportunity thoroughly to study and digest the question from every angle.

I have a short memorandum on this subject here which I will read first:
The question of revaluation is one that is creating considerable interest, and it is worth while explaining what is being done.
The act was passed a year ago, becoming effective on the 1st June. The condition of the act was that a settler had up to the 1st October, 1927, to apply for revaluation. As there were a number who had not applied at that time, an order in council was passed lengthening the time to the 30th November, 1927, with a proviso that if special conditions arose in which a settler was unable to make application, and these conditions were submitted to the board under oath, the board might accept his application for revaluation.
It was quite evident that before revaluation could be systematically and economically carried out, it would be necessary to wait until the greater number of applications had been received, so that a district could be plotted out and revaluation undertaken without the loss of too much time and too great expense.
It was first decided that no revaluation would be started until all the applications were in, but as the applications came in more rapidly than was expected, it was decided that revaluation should start during July, 1927, and be proceeded with until winter conditions made it impossible to make a proper revaluation.
The method of revaluation is that the land inspector making the revaluation proceeded to the settler's place, and, in conference with the settler, agreed to the identity of the land, the state of cultivation in which the land was when it was bought for him, and the condition of the buildings when bought. This having been agreed to, the inspector proceeded to measure up the acreages that were under cultivation and those which were cultivable, and also to make other appraisements on the land and put a valuation on the buildings, as they were at that time. Having done this, the inspector then placed a valuation on the farm as it was when purchased, according to present day values in that particular district.
The act also provided that if a settler had, by good farming methods, brought his land into a better state of cultivation than it was when he got it, then he received an allowance in appreciation, but if it was discovered that the land was in a fair to good state of cultivation when he got it but by neglect and poor farming it had gone back, then he was charged up with a certain amount of depreciation.
If buildings had been removed, the settler was charged up with the price of the buildings, or if buildings had been burned he was charged up with the amount of insurance that he had received, or, in other words, if a piece of land

When the question came before the house, on the report of the railway committee and the amendment thereto, the Minister of Railways made the following statement, as reported at page 2409 of Hansard, April, 13, 1927:
I intimated while the hon. member was speaking that the government was prepared to accede to that request if the amendment now before the house were withdrawn; and indeed, whether it is withdrawn or not-my hon. friend can press it to a vote if he desires-the government does intend in any event to secure further detailed engineering information lin order to be able to say to the people of the

In view of that statement I want the minister to tell us what has been done in the way of carrying it into effect. It has been said for years that the Peace river pass is the best route. That may or may not be so, but the late Premier Oliver of British Columbia advocated a line through the Peace pass to Prince George as the best method solving the Peace River Railway problem. His words can be found at page 46 of the evidence of the committee on railways of 1927, The Minister of the Interior was also of that opinion and his words touching the matter are reported at page 270 of Hansard of last year, when he said:
I agree with the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) that the only feasible route, irrespective of what it costs, is by the Peace river pass. No one can deny that who knows the topography of the country and the direction in which the rivers run.
The report of the joint board of engineers of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway on various proposed railway routes for a western outlet to the Pacific from the Peace river district contains the following on page 7:
In considering a western outlet from Peace River district (to avoid back-haul) two branches will be required; one starting at Spirit river and running westward 165 miles to Rocky Mountain canyon when it and the branch from Berwyn 200 miles long form a junction on south side of Peace river, this being the only practical crossing of Peace river.
The gradient of new line along the Peace river need not exceed 0.4 per cent excepting the
branch on south side from Spirit river to junction at Rocky Mountain canyon, which will require 1.00 per cent gradient.
The line for about 150 miles west of Berwyn on north side of Peace river is through country that in time would become agricultural, and the same can be said for the first 125 miles west of Spirit river excepting the part through forest reserve.
No extraordinary difficulties would be encountered in construction of line along Peace river; the work would be classed as heavy if compare with average prairie line, and light if compared with average mountain lines.
From Rocky Mountain canyon to Prince George (257 miles) the line will closely parallel the Peace river to Mount Selwyn, thence up the Parsnip, the Pack and Crooked rivers to Summit lake, thence down the slope of Fraser river to Prince George, 35 miles.
From Prince George the traffic can be carried over several routes.
Mr. Hill, who was one of the engineers who signed that report, found that matters were not quite as stated in the report, although I must say his findings are not very conclusive. In paragraph 4 of his report he has this to say:
Range 15 to Rocky Mountain canyon (southerly route). The best and largest area of agricultural land in the Peace river block, north of the river, is known as the St. John country and is in elevation 1,000 feet, or more above the Peace river. To the east of it the Beatton river runs south into the Peace river and its valley is 600 to 1,000 feet deep. To cross it with a direct line gradients up to 2.0 per cent would be required.
The last report stated one per cent. I do not know that I need take up any more of the time of the committee at present with this report, but while the statements with regard to Peace pass and the other passes were made in good faith, we find that the more they are investigated the more new facts come out, which neither the engineers nor anyone else thoroughly grasped previously. It should be pointed out that Mr. Hill's report of last year is mainly concerned1 with the railway running between Whitelaw, the present end of the Central Canada Railway, to Hudson Hope cm the north side of the Peace river. It does not cover the Peace pass, which begins at Hudson Hope. Mr. Hill states that to construct a line coming close to the Peace river on the north side would require gradients of 2 per cent, but that a longer route swinging north would require gradients of only one per cent. However, his report does not state the extra cost which would be involved or the extra mileage which the longer route would necessitate, and in view of that fact the last statement of his report is very much in point. It says:
The Obed route, from information available, is unquestionably the best Pacific outlet for the

Peace River country as a whole. It is, however, unpopular with certain sections of the country. Actual surveys have been made over this route and also the Pine pass route. In order that a correct comparison may be made-
That is the point.
-between all routes, surveys must be made over the other two, the Monkman pass and Peace pass routes.
Notwithstanding the fact that the engineer gives certain conclusions and says that this route is not as good as the other, he admits that he has not complete and correct information, and that the information cannot be correct until it is complete. I would like to see complete surveys made of the Peace pass and Monkman pass routes. With all due respect to the engineers and without questioning their good faith I submit that we cannot make a comparison between these various routes until we have a similar or practically similar survey of the Peace pass and Monkman pass routes. I think the experience this country has had as a result of duplication of railways and wrong locations of railways in the past, leading to permanently increased costs of operation and fixed charges, should indicate that it is a wise policy to make sure of the proper location of an outlet such as this.
There is one result which I think is obvious from the survey work already done. I think it was shown in the report of the committee last year that the Peace river country could be railroaded in such a way as to provide about 6,000 economic acres of land to every mile of railway as against about 5,000 acres or a little more in the three prairie provinces. That will mean a great deal in connection with the operation and the revenues of the railway in the future. A survey of these passes may cost several thousand dollars, but the wrong location of railways-because when a railway is once put down it cannot be moved -or the construction of excessive gradients where lower gradients might be obtained at a reasonable cost, soon add millions of dollars which must be paid by the people of the country in freight rates. So I submit that while it may cost a little more to survey these passes, and while we might save a few thousand dollars by not making these surveys, it would be much better to spend that money and get a correct location which will give us the cheapest possible cost of operation in the future. If that policy had been followed in laying out the railways throughout the three prairie provinces as well as throughout the rest of Canada; if a comprehensive study such as will be made if these surveys in the 
Peace river country are completed had been made in the three prairie provinces, it would have meant a great saving in connection with our Canadian National railways. So I submit that it is good policy for Canada and good policy for the Canadian National Railways or any other railway company to have that information, and since in the last analysis the cost of mistakes in railway construction and operation will come directly or indirectly, out of the pockets of the people of Canada, I think it would be a wise and ultimately economic thing for the minister to carry out at the earliest possible moment the promise he made last year.

However, they are also aware of the fact that a coast outlet would place them in a position as advantageous with respect to shipping their grain to the Pacific coast as that occupied by Edmonton to-day, and the saving in the cost of moving grain to the Pacific coast as against the cost from Edmonton would be approximately 6 cents per bushel. As another member of this house who is more or less interested in the development of the Peace River country, I would like to say a very few words in regard to this question. I might say at the outset that I am rather disappointed in the statement of the Minister of Railways. My hon. friend (Mr. Kennedy) has just quoted it; there is no question about it.

I intimated while the hon. member was speaking that the government was prepared to accede to that request .if the amendment now before the house were withdrawn; and, indeed, whether it is withdrawn or not-my hon. friend can press it to a vote if he desires-the government does intendin any event to secure further detailed engineering information in order to be able to say to the people of the Peace river country and to the people of British Columbia, who are vitally affected, "When a western outlet is built, this in our opinion is the pass through which that line of railway should be constructed." Just by way of introduction I would like to say this; let the house remember in the first place that we are dealing with a very large question. The Peace River drainage basin comprises 117,000 square miles of land, which is equal to about 75,000,000 acres. In my opinion, with this land it is possible to double the present output of wheat in the Dominion of Canada. Anything that will do that is surely an important question and one that requires the very earnest attention of every person in the Dominion of Canada. It would indicate that by the development of the Peace River country it is possible almost to double the population of the Dominion of Canada.
Let me point out this further fact. The Peace River country is roughly a thousand miles from the Pacific Ocean and three thousand miles from the Atlantic seaboard. That would surely indicate that the best route to haul the products of that country is to the west. At once another question comes in, and that is the Panama canal. The Panama canal is having a wonderful effect all over the Pacific coast. At the present time we

are actually transporting goods from Toronto and Hamilton to the city of Vancouver without breaking bulk. So far as I am concerned the proper route to be taken is via the Peace River valley. This route would provide the lowest grades through the Rocky mountains. That is not on the Peace

Anyone who will attempt to make parliament or the people of the Dominion of Canada believe that that report has any relation at all to the Peace River country's western outlet is not putting the matter in a proper light. I might as well take up that question now. The Peace River country, to be properly served, must have a main line from the coast to Hudson Hope. From Hudson Hope there must be two lines, one on the north side of the river and one on the south side. The work that was done by your engineer this year did not touch the Peace River pass at all. It went as far as Hudson Hope and it went from there east to Peace River crossing or somewhere near there. It linked up those two points. That is only branch line construction and it will be so for all time in the Peace River country. Exactly the same thing pertains to the south side of the river. There will be one mainline running from the Pacific coast to Hudson Hope and from that point we must have a branch line on each side of the river. That will be branch line construction and operation for all time.
Then how are the Peace River people going to get mainline service?

The mainline from the
Peace River is from the coast to Hudson Hope. From that point you must have two lines. Let me say this also in connection with the Peace River. That is the only route into the Peace River country that will not entail a back haul. On any other route you take, for instance, the Obed route, the Monkman route, or any of the southern routes, you will have to haul the freight on the north side of the river either to Berwyn on the east or to Hudson Hope on the west. It is impossible to suppose that either of those areas will remain undeveloped. Consequently the development of the Peace River country in my opinion must be through the Peace River pass, because that is the only route which will not entail a back haul and of course add distance to the haul and add to the expense of the haul. only provide railway service for a very limited area in the Peace River country. In fact I had a letter from a man telling me that if he had teams working from the time that sleighing was in shape to haul the grain and would keep at it until the sleighing was finished, he would have two or three thousand bushels of grain that it would be impossible for him to haul during that year. All this makes it a slow proposition to haul the grain of that country to the railway terminal which is at Spirit river. These men are paying thirty cents a bushel for hauling this grain to the railway. I was told of one instance where they came to a river. There had been a chinook wind a day or two before, and the water was running over the ice. The man had to haul his load of grain over the ice, and the water on top of the ice was so deep that it flooded his sleigh and wet his grain, and when he got to Spirit river, the elevator would net accept his grain because it was wet. The minister disclaimed any responsibility for the combined offer. I submit that if that proposition is gone about in a proper and comprehensive way, the development of that Peace river country will absolutely wipe out all deficits on the Canadian National Railways. I submit that I am not asking too much when I ask the minister to have a comprehensive survey made of all the conditions by an eminent engineer who will bring in a definite and final report that will enable the people of Canada to know exactly what should be done in order to open up that country.

I shall not follow in any way the lines that have been taken by the two hon. gentlemen wtho have just spoken. But I wish to place before the house, in the five minutes I intend to take, a question involving the responsibility that is absolutely on the shoulders of this government, and that is to implement what they themselves commenced. The Prime Minister himself, in words that certainly conveyed only one meaning, placed himself definitely behind this outlet to the Pacific coast for the Peace river country. The Minister of Railways last year, also in words as emphatic as a man could use, pledged himself to do what his words were intended to convey. They are in Hansard; shall I read them?
Dispense.

I am glad the house knows exactly what the Minister of Railways said In the short time at my disposal I will us? the logic which the Champions of the Hudson bay railway used to get that road completed to the stage in which it is in to-day. I went to the trouble of reading their speeches, and here are the arguments they advanced for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, and if these arguments are not tenfold stronger for an outlet to the Pacific coast fo-the Peace river country, then our logic is at fault and our arguments are vain. Here are the arguments which the champions of the Hudson Bay railway used:
1 That a huge sum had already been expended. and that to abandon the railway would be a great -waste of public money.
Now here is the first parallel. It was this Dominion government that placed thousands of settlers in the Peace river valley. They are still coming in and will settle there permanently. It is the duty of the government to implement what they promised. Now, number two:
That large area3 in Saskatchewan and Manitoba were set aside and the proceeds from their sale were earmarked for this special enterprise.
In regard to this we already have large sums expended on the reconnaissance and survey of the Obed, Pine and Monkman passes. The Peace River pass has yet to be surveyed in accordance with the people's views. We have spent money there already. Are we going to stop now, when for *he last three months we have been dealing with the biggest problem that confronts the Canadian people -immigration? It is part and parcel of that very scheme. The duty of the government is to decide for all time to come where that outlet is to be and so set the minds of the people at rest. I am not advocating one outlet or the other, but I demand that the minister define the outlet. When that is done you can put in your subsidiary lines wherever necessary. The third argument advanced for the Hudson Bay railway was this:
That the route was feasible on the ground of safety of navigation and shortening of transportation.
Now I appeal to the committee, is not that argument conclusive to-day regarding the Peace River outlet? There is a big drawback by the Edmonton and Dunvegan line to Edmonton. To get that route to the Pacific coast is just as important for the farmers of Alberta and British Columbia as is the Hudson Bay line for the farmers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We were told that if the Hudson Bay railway were connected up at Port Nelson-since Fort Churchill-the terminal would be the same distance from Liverpool as Montreal is, namely, three thousand miles. If that be true, and if that was the main argument for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, I say unhesitatingly that that argument is tenfold stronger when we advance it to get the shortest and most economical route from the Peace river country to the Pacific coast.
Another argument brought forward was found in the wonderful history of the Temis-kaming and Northern Ontario railway, and it was said that the Hudson Bay line would equal it because of the great mineral territory through which it would run. Will any hon. gentleman dare deny that the mineral wealth

I have just one question
to ask the minister, a question which is often asked by the man on the street who is not well versed in economics and high finance. How is it that the management of the Canadian National Railways claim to have surpluses and yet to-night we are asked to vote an amount of S39,000,000? If these surpluses exist why must we vote money for the use of the Canadian National Railways this year?

The answer to that question is very simple. When the term "surplus" is used in connection with railway operation it means a surplus of revenue over the expenses of operation. There still remains to be paid the interest on the capital obligations of the railway, and the deficit in connection with the Canadian National Railway arises because of the fact that, until the present, it has not earned enough over and above its operating expenses to pay the interest upon all its bonded indebtedness. In recent times it has generally succeeded in earning sufficient to pay the interest upon that portion of its obligations held by the public.
Only in one year.

I am making a general
statement; if we combine the last two years it has practically carried itself as far as interest due the public is concerned, but I am ready to let my hon. friend have his own view in that regard. In general, having regard to the size of the figures involved, it may be said that the Canadian National Railway is now earning sufficient to pay interest on the obligations held by the public.

And if a member wants
some information about the affairs of the Canadian National Railways would it be poc-sible for him to get that information, even in a confidential way?

That is a very difficult
question to answer without knowing what kind of information is desired.

Any kind of information,
because we are voting money and we should know where it goes.

When I made way for
the minister about an hour ago I was about to direct his attention to the fact that the Canadian National Railway system is not giving an adequate service to the people of the district which I represent. We are called upon to-night to vote the sum of 839,000,000 to this company, and surely it is the duty of every member of parliament to see that this money is spent in the interest of service to the whole people of Canada. I speak as one who is most anxious to see the Canadian National Railways succeed in every way, and I believe the minister is most anxious to see that the railway gives service to every section of the country. Therefore I call his attention to the fact that in the county of Renfrew the Canadian National Railways are not giving a satisfactory and sufficient service.
In the first place, through a peculiar and penurious policy which has been practised for the last few years, by cutting down the maintenance of way men they have left the roadbed in such a condition that at times it is very dangerous to travel over that section by train. Not only is that the case, but the railway station at Caldwell in the county of Renfrew, a most important centre, was burned down two years ago. Since then they have been transacting business in a box car, and at that it is not one of the large box cars but one of the smallest of those built within the last twenty-five years. During these two years a great deal of business has been transacted at this point; month after month more than 810,000, 812,000 and 815,000 in revenue has gone into the coffers of the railway company from outgoing and incoming traffic, but the box car still remains. Conditions are such that the health authorities of that municipality are considering closing that box car because they believe it unfit for human habitation ; under the provincial law they have power to do so. In addition to that, in the westerly part of the county of Renfrew it takes three days to make a round trip between two points only thirty miles apart. Any man who is not crippled could walk the distance in much less time. I draw these facts to the attention of the minister and ask him to impress them upon the management of the Canadian National Railway system. They have been brought to the attention of the management many times ,but I ask the minister now, feeling that he is anxious to see that all sections of the country are properly served by this railway, to bring these facts to the attention of the management.

I shall be glad to do so.

I realize that it is not a very popular thing for a member to make a speech at this stage of the session, and particularly when it originates from what the press of the country calls a "back bencher." However, I am going to take a few moments of the time of the house to bring up a matter which not only interests the section of the country which I have the honour to repre-t sent but affects the whole of Canada. I refer to the principle of taxation which is applied to the Canadian National Railway system. When last Wednesday I brought up this subject before the committee, the Minister of Railways asked me if I would bring it up again when we were dealing with the Canadian National Railways supplementary estimates. I hope that hon. members will be indulgent towards me because so far this session I have listened a lot and said very little.
Another factor is that we in northern Ontario very seldom come before this house asking for favours, but the moment I received the mandate to represent that section of northern Ontario I knew I was bound to present this matter before the house, as it is one we have been agitating for for the last twelve years. We have sent several delegations to the different ministers of railways, and the different governments, and our public bodies have met the premiers both of the Dominion and of the province. I want to make it clear at the very outset that it is not my intention to make this a political matter, because I expect to get support from every section of this house.
Eighty per cent of the Canadian National railway system is actually paying taxes, or compensation, if you prefer the word, and the other twenty per cent is not. Of the same substance eighty per cent is called flesh and twenty per cent is called fish. This twenty per cent is through the northern part of the country, and I feel I am bound to bring this matter before the house as forcibly as possible. It has been previously said that public and private ownership are going to remain with us. We are not against the principle of public ownership in northern Ontario, but we should receive the help that other parts of the province are obtaining from that public ownership. The first thing that comes to one's mind when dealing with public or private ownership is the matter of taxation. I know the house will look reluctantly on the principle of voting public money to pay taxes to a section of the country in respect to a part of the road actually owned by the government. When I mention Cochrane or northern

Ontario, I do not want to be regarded as taking any local or regional attitude; as I said at the outset, I want to consider this matter in a non-political and national sense.
On the 12th of January last, I wrote a letter to the Minister of Railways telling him of my intention to place before this house a motion to generalize the system of taxation on the whole railroad. I will read his answer:
I appreciate very much your advising me in advance of your intention to move a resolution in the House of Commons having to do with the Canadian National Railways.	_
As you know, the whole subject is a very complex one and includes widely differing conditions in different parts of the country. You will pardon my pointing out one error in your letter and that is the statement that the National Transcontinental line is practically the only part of the Canadian National system not actually paying municipal and school taxes. As a matter of fact, no municipal or school taxes are paid by the system in Saskatchewan or Alberta and I believe also in a considerable portion of Manitoba; also, no taxes are paid in the maritime provinces on the former Intercolonial lines. This will serve to indicate to you the magnitude and complexity of the problem.
Through my activities during the last twelve years as a member of the municipal council of the town of Cochrane and also a member of the associated boards of trade of northern Ontario, I have taken a very important part in the discussion on that all-important question. I realize that this is a really complicated problem, nevertheless an injustice is always an injustice; and an injustice has been perpetrated and perpetuated against northern Ontario.
At the present time practically 80 per cent of the system pays taxes, mostly in the towns and cities and in the most thickly populated centres of the country, and that principle should be generalized, more particularly over that section of the road from Quebec to Winnipeg. When I was speaking last Wednesday a member of the opposite side of the house asked me about the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was stated at the last annual meeting of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that they actually paid to the municipal and provincial governments of the country nearly $8,000,000 in taxation. I would assume from that that the Canadian Pacific Railway is paying taxation on the whole system.

I believe he was right in that regard, because the principles or policies of taxation of public utilities should emanate from Ottawa so that we may know exactly how taxation will be applied and generalized so that we would not be characterized by the hit-and-miss system under which we are working at the present time. We have spent a good deal of time to-day in discussion, but we have not made as much progress as we had hoped to be able to make. I gather that hon. members are anxious that the session shall not be unduly prolonged and I imagine that we could make more progress if we sat somewhat later this evening. I would therefore move:
That the house shall not be adjourned at eleven o'clock p.m. this day.
That does not mean an unlimited sitting?

No, but it gives latitude for progress if we are making progress.
