Motion agreed to.

I beg to lay on the table the report of the joint committee on the library of parliament, which met on May 31, 1928, as follows:
The committee authorized the transfer of the volumes of the Irish Law Reports series to the Department of Justice, and also of certain technical books to the library of the mines department, with the understanding that such books should be accessible to members of parliament at any time.
As a result of a discussion on the question of the laxity in respect to the return of library books, the following resolution was unanimously passed:
"That, when members of parliament have in their possession more than six library books, and when such books are retained in their possession for such a period of time as to inconvenience other members who may desire to borrow such books, then it shall be the duty of the liibrarians to notify the members that, by order of the joint committee on the library, the books must be promptly returned, and, if not so returned, the librarians are hereby instructed to report the case to the committee, or to the speakers."
A question was asked respecting the case of an ex-member of parliament who for a long time had had in his possession a number of books from the parliamentary library and, though notified on several occasions, had neither answered the librarian's letter nor returned the books. The committee unanimously passed the following resolution:
"That, the librarians are hereby instructed to communicate with the ex-member in question, and to inform him that these library books now in his possession are the property of the crown, and that, as he had been notified to return them and had ignored such notice, unless such books are returned immediately after this final notice, the matter will be placed iii the hands of the Justice department with the request to take action to recover the property." _

I hope that next year,
I will be given an opportunity to thresh this question out very thoroughly before the railway committee. The matter is complicated and there is a great deal of information which would be very useful to the house to enable it to study the problem fully. That is why I am going to cut my speech very short.
As I said before, I have received a considerable number of answers to the circulars and pamphlets sent to members of parliament and also to members of the provincial legislature.
I am going to read only one of them a letter from Senator G. D. Robertson, which is very typical of those which I have received. That is what he has to say about the matter under date of February 14, 1923:
Dear Sir:
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 8th inst., together with printed circular enclosed referring to the desirability of the Canadian National railways being assessed for municipal and school purposes.
At Cochrane and other points along the Transcontinental where the railway property represents a large portion of the improved property in the municipality I readily appreciate the propriety of the railway bearing some of the cost of municipal taxation, especially for schools, as most of the children attending such schools are children of employees of the railway company and such employees ought not to be taxed for school purposes more heavily than are similar employees in other municipalities where the proportion of taxation is more widely distributed. This question was discussed some two years ago by the late government, being brought to its attention by the undersigned after my return from Winnipeg in August 1920 via the Transcontinental railway, when this question was brought to my attention, but it was not deemed advisable to take action at that time, or until the whole of the government-owned lines were merged into one system. Now that this is being done and the Grand Trunk and Canadian Northern portions of the Canadian National system do not pay taxes, there would seem to be no good reason why some reasonable rate of taxation should not also be imposed upon the portions of the national system formerly known as the Canadian Government railways.
I shall be glad to lend such aid as I may be able to bring some relief to your municipality, and others similarly situated, but feel that the movement should be initiated in the House of Commons, as the jurisdiction of the Senate, of which I am a member, respecting the introduction of money bills might be questioned.
I have at least a hundred letters, all very sympathetic. Here is one from Mr. Manion, another from Mr. William Irvine, another from Mayor Lavigueur to Mir. Warrell, clerk of the municipality of Cochrane. They show that the matter was discussed, if not on the floor of this house at least among the members, and most of them were very sympathetic. I hope that an opportunity will be given me to explain the situation before the railway .committee. I realize that it is getting late in the session to get a grant of money, but again I ask the Minister of Railways if that amount of $75,000 is still in the possession of the government. If so, that distribution should be made at once during the year 1928. We have the machin-
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

ery and all the organization necessary to take care of the distribution of that money.
We in that section of northern Ontario are willing and ready to help all other sections of the country. We have shown it in the past. We are not numerous, but the time is coming when that section will contain millions of people. More and more we are becoming the treasure house of the North American continent; but just now we' are in the pioneering stage and we must insist in our demands for what is legitimately coming to us. For these reasons I am asking for support on this all-important question to us, and that we get this compensation as soon as possible. We are willing to go without sidewalks, or to put up with very bad ones. We will do without good streets, but we want our children to have proper school accommodation. We want them to have good qualified teachers. We want them to have at least a good elementary and high school education. We do not want their location to be against their education. I believe that in helping out section you will be helping particularly the cause of education in this country. In conclusion, I hope that something will be done, and in the very near future, to alleviate the injustice that has been done to that section of the country during the last twelve years.

I might just briefly say in reply to my hon. friend that the question of taxation of all the various units comprising the Canadian National railway system is, as I indicated in the letter which he read, a very complex problem. Certain lines are crown lines, and always have been, and because of that fact they have been exempt from taxation. Certain others were owned by private companies, now forming part of the Canadian National railway system.

And were exempt from
taxation by statute.

Yes, and certain others were privately owned, and were not exempt from taxation at all. Then there is still another class in the west which are exempt from municipal and school taxes because of the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway exemption from similar taxation applies all over the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and over a part of the province of Manitoba. This brief statement will illustrate the great difficulty of the problem.
A little over a year ago, on an occasion when the various provinces were represented, an effort was made by the Canadian National Railway to reach some common ground of

agreement between the provinces, and it was thought that such agreement had been reached. Subsequently, however, two or three of the provinces indicated that the understanding which iit was really thought had been arrived at did not coincide with their view of what was done at the conference, and consequently the situation still remains very complex indeed. I do not wanlt to go into a lengthy discussion of it to-night.
My hon. friend indicated something which I will suggest to the members of the house generally, and that is that when the special committee on railways and shipping is in session, the committee before which these estimates were presented and considered in detail, an excellent opportunity is afforded to members of the house generally to present before that committee any case such as that now presented by my hon. friend from North Timiskaming, on an occasion when the general officers of the company, with the necessary records and information, are there for the very purpose of giving information to the parliamentary committee. I suggest that the time of the house can be saved if members generally will take advantage of the presence in Ottawa of the general officers of the company attending the meetings of the special committee. That applies also to my hon. friend from South Renfrew, who spoke of some matter of train service, information regarding which cannot possibly be in the possession of the minister, or of any of the departmental officers available to the minister when the estimates are before the house; but these matters can be considered in detail before the committee.
In conclusion, may I say this? The situation with respect to the National Transcontinental is a peculiarly acute one, and while we are trying to solve it in common with all the other problems of a similar nature from coast to coast, I can only say that I will undertake to see to it that that phase of the problem receives during the recess consideration separately from the rest, in view of the fact that we have been unable to reach an agreement, with the provinces comprehensive enough to cover the whole of the problems which require to be dealt with in regard to taxation. I trust that my hon. friend will be satisfied with the assurance that this particular phase will be examined during the recess.

That is satisfactory, but I would ask the minister if it is not possible to have a distribution of that sum of $75,000 this year. We have all the necessary

equipment and organization, municipally speaking, to take care of that amount, which should be given to the municipalities direct and not to the province.
I will see to it that consideration is given to that phase of the question.

Again this year we are
asked to vote a very large sum of money to the Canadian National railway, involving an increase over last year of some $17,239,500. I think perhaps the people of this country are not worrying very much about voting this amount of money so long as they feel that they are getting a good return from the investment.
I would ask the Minister of Railways, who has just undertaken on behalf of one of the members of his party, to do something, if he will undertake to see to it that we have presented to us next year, if we are spared to come back to this House of Commons, a balance sheet, setting out the assets and the liabilities of the Canadian National railway system, which will be a true reflection as nearly as possible of what is taking place and of what has taken place during the last five years. To make it as brief as I possibly can, due to the lateness of the session, we one and all know that there have been vast amounts of money spent on capital account for the Canadian National Railways, more particularly during the last five years, expenditures on road and equipment which in turn apply to the asset side of this balance sheet. The investments on capital account this year total $43,724,677.16, bringing the grand total up to $1,914,000,000. Just let that sink into the minds of hon. members a little bit. There has been invested in road and equipment, and charged holus bolus to capital account, $1,914,000,000 and not one dollar of that, apart from the retirements from year 'to year, has been written off that vast capital for exhaustion of the different units which go to make up the system. Not one dollar has been written off for exhaustion and depreciation. The only amount that has been written off is the amount representing the original cost of some item which was retired. That is written off, but nothing else. The minister well knows that the class A roads in the United States, in accordance with the regulations of the Interstate Commerce Commission, write off a certain amount each year for exhaustion or depreciation, if you will. The minister well knows that that portion of our road which operates in the United States under
the Interstate Commerce Commission must write off a certain amount for exhaustion or depreciation, and yet we in Canada are being more or less led astray by this balance sheet which does not show any reflection of the exhaustion or depreciation on the many hun- _ dreds of millions of dollars which have been poured into the road in the form of new equipment. I would be the last man to attempt to demoralize that great institution, the Canadian National Railways. I am anxious to forward its interests to the very best of my ability, but I owe a duty to the people I represent to point out that this balance sheet is not a true reflection of what is happening in regard to the system. True, in fifty years' time as we retire the different elements which go to make up this system to-day we shall come back to the stage where the total capital account may show the original cost of everything that makes up the road. But would it not be fairer to ourselves and to the country at large if year by year we reflected in this statement some idea of the amount of exhaustion which is taking place? To my mind the Minister of Railways will be doing a service to the country if he demands that the railway commission exercise jurisdiction-if they have any-over the accounts of the Canadian National Railways so that the balance sheet may show a fair reflection of the depreciation. I would ask the minister at least to give us a ray of hope that this will be done.

Mr. Chairman, I wish
to address a few remarks to the Minister of Railways. Our division of the Canadian National Railways from Ste. Rosalie to Riviere du Loup, comprising 250 miles, in 1925 and 1926 gave a total revenue of eleven million dollars, and the expenses were only seven million dollars. There are no important places along the line. Its cost being valued at $40,000 a mile would bring the total for that mileage to ten million dollars. Now, the net revenue being four million dollars, if you allow interest or dividend at 5 per cent it would mean $500,000. In other words, our division has paid over and above that 5 per cent $3,500,000 to the country. And we are not saying a word. We are only asking the minister, not to open new roads, not to give us new stations, but just to keep the present road and stations and equipment in good condition. We are paying 20 peT cent on the capital investment in our division. I repeat, we only ask the minister to keep the property in good condition, and we hope members
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

from other parts of the country will be satisfied, as we are, to wait until their divisions pay 20 per cent on the investment before they ask for further expenditure.

I desire to add a few
words in support of the remarks of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Maloney), as to the condition of the railway service along what was formerly known as the Canada Atlantic division of the Grand Trunk, now under the control of the Canadian National Railways. Originally there was a daily service from Ottawa to Depot Harbour or Parry Sound. This service has been reduced to two trips a week from Ottawa to Scotia Junction. I have no objection to that at all. I do not want the railway to put on a service that does not pay. But on the remainder of the line, some fifty or sixty miles, from Scotia Junction to Depot Harbour, the service is by a mixed train daily each way. The car set aside for the service of the public must I think have been the first car built by the Grand Trunk Railway. It is lighted by old coal oil lamps, which I am sure are forty or fifty years old, and they only make the darkness visible. You cannot read, you cannot write, you cannot do anything to pass the time on this train which jogs along at night. The heating system is on a par with the lighting. I am quite sure that if the minister saw this car he would immediately see that it was replaced by one of the many modern cars lying idle at other places. As a matter of fact, this daily service covers a well-populated section of fifty miles. The service itself is not unsatisfactory in regard to time, but we ask that proper equipment be supplied, or that an electric car replece the present equipment.

I wish to support the remarks by the hon. gentleman from Levis (Mr. Dussault). It is only fair that those sections of the line which provide revenue should receive consideration. It would save the house a half hour speech if the minister would be kind enough to ask the deputy minister to tell Sir Henry Thornton that the town of Oshawa-which contributes a larger percentage to the revenues of the Canadian National Railway system than any other place of its size-has the most inadequate, most unhealthy, most unsanitary and most antiquated station along the line.

I regret that the Canadian 'National Railway estimates have been left until now for consideration, and that this item has been held over until such a late day

in the session. The Minister of Railways, speaking a few moments ago, informed hon. members that the proper place to take up problems in relation to railways would be in the select committee on railways and shipping. I understood that committee was appointed for an ,entirely different purpose, and any member, not a member of that committee, has not the privilege of addressing it except by permission due to some sittings being held in camera.

On mo occasion in the past two years has the request of any member of the house, not a member of the committee, been refused by the committee for permission to be heard with respect to any matter. That is the custom in the committee.

I am glad to get that information. I understand now that by courtesy we have the privilege of appearing before the committee. I shall very briefly bring to the attention of this committee a matter of considerable importance, and I offer mo apologies for so doing even at this late hour. We have listened with a great deal of pleasure to railway propositions with regard to the Peace River district and also in the northern Ontario district, and for a few moments I shall direct the attention of the minister and the bouse to the want of railways in the east.
A year ago, when the Minister of Railways brought down his three year branch line railway program, which if I remember correctly called for some $10,000,000 for railways in the west, he made the statement that the door was not closed and that possibly at some future time, before the three year program had been completed, he would do something for the people in eastern Canada. We need four branch lines in the province of Nova Scotia, but I shall confine my remarks very briefly to one in my constituency, the Steiwiacke valley railway. The hiistory of this road dates back so far that there is not a member in this house, I believe who has any recollection of such a railway. In the year 1888 a company was formed to build a branch line railway through that valley, beginning at a point on the main line, going in a direct line through a very fertile valley and connecting with the main line at another point. I am giving this information for the benefit of the Minister of Railways who has just recently told us that he arrived in this country twenty-five years ago. He will see that fifteen years before he came here this proposed railway was under construction. As I stated, the company was formed in the year 1888 and the usual

Supply-Railvrays-C.N.R.
incorporating bill passed the provincial legislature at that time. It required a paid up capital of 850,000 in the treasury before the company could apply to the provincial or federal governments for subsidies. That amount was in the treasury, and with a certificate or receipt from the bankers, they proceeded to England and sold their bonds. The farmers along the Stewiacke valley, who were well-to-do farmers, subscribed heavily to that company. The promoters began construction work, and ten miles of road was graded. As I stated, the history of this undertaking goes so far back that I am unable to give to the house the precise reason why the moneys to be realized by sale of bonds in England were not available for the prosecution and completion of the work. But suddenly, without warning, operations on the construction work were discontinued. The result was that the bondholders in England sent a man over to make investigations and it was discovered that aM they had to represent an advance of some $300,000 was a right of way thirty-five miles long, with ten miles graded. I regret that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is not in his seat as he was at that time solicitor for the English bondholders. They discovered that the shareholders of the company, who were largely farmers throughout the Stewiacke valley, were liable to the bondholders for the amount of their shares. The shareholders appealed to the government of Nova Scotia, who after considerable delay came forward and liquidated the debts due to the English bondholders, thus relieving the shareholders of a liability amounting to $300,000. Consequently the provincial government owns the right of way, of which ten miles are graded.
The Minister of Railways has had a resolution placed in his hands indicating the possibilities of that road as a revenue producer. I have a copy of that resolution. I will not detain ithe committee by reading it. Let me say, however, that in addition to what is therein set forth I have a letter from a wealthy American lumber concern who have purchased something like 90,000 acres of land on the Stewiacke river, on which they state they have approximately 125,000,000 board feet of hardwood that cannot be driven downstream and must be moved by rail. If the Minister of Railways will be good enough to come to our province this summer and give me the pleasure of taking him through this magnificent valley, and meet its people who are the salt of the earth, I will also show him the greatest deposit of gravel in the whole of Nova Scotia. As the Canadian National
Railways are building branch lines into gravel deposits, I can show the minister a deposit which is unsurpassed in any part of this country. This has not been set forth in the resolution presented to the government.

If it will help my hon. friend and relieve him of the necesrity of making a further plea, I can assure him that before any further branch line program is submitted by the management to the minister, the minister will request the management to go carefully into the Stewiacke valley situation. If it will shorten the discussion with respect to branch lines and with respect to certain railway acquisitions which have been brought to my attention by members on all sides of the house, I wish to give the same general assurance regarding them all. There will be a careful examination, and the very fact that my hon. friend has mentioned it again will ensure this being done. With respect to my hon, friends from Levis, Parry Sound and Ontario, who have in their midst at least according to their own ideas, such splendidly paying sections of the Canadian National, I can only say that if the figures they present prove to be correct there is no question but that sections of the railways earning so handsomely should receive any necessary attention. I am sure my remarks in this connection will catch the eye of the president and will result in the figures presented by hon. members being very closely examined.
With respect to my hon. friend from Toronto-Scarborough, at this late hour I shall not attempt to enter a discussion of the accounting methods employed by the Canadian National Railways. I will content myself by saying that a reference by any member of this committee to the evidence taken before the select standing committee on railways and shipping, a copy of which has been placed in the hands of every hon. member of the house, will reveal that my hon. friend from Toronto-Scarborough went into the matter of accounting very fully and very fairly, if I may say so, with the accounting officers, the general officers and the president of the company before that committee. Opinions very easily differ on the question of accounting; I think that, fact is well realized by all members of this committee who have had any experience in business matters. I can only say to my hon. friend that for myself I intend to study very carefully the representations he made before that committee together with his remarks here to-night, and I know the officers of the company responsible in that connec-

tion will do the same thing because already it has been a matter of discussion among them since the conclusion of the sessions of that committee. I think that is all I can say at the moment.

While the minister is
giving consideration to the Parry Sound district and to Oshawa I want to draw his attention to the station of Sunnyside, four miles west of the union station in Toronto. I would say that 75 per cent of the people travelling west from Toronto get on at Sunny-side station. There the station building is away up on a hill; you have to go across a poorly constructed bridge and then down thirty or forty steps to a great open space. There people must stand fifteen or twenty minutes waiting for trains, with no protection against rain or other weather conditions. Some consideration should be given to the people who use that station. I have waited there for fifteen or twenty minutes in the rain and snow; there is no place to sit down or even stand under shelter. I drew this matter to the attention of the deputy minister two years ago and I was promised some relief, but so far the station people tell me nothing has been done. I would ask the minister not to try to remember this without making a note of it, 'because these things are easily forgotten and I am afraid a lot of the ministers opposite forget purposely.

We are not allowed to
forget anything that goes into Hansard, and the remarks of my hon. friend are going into Hansard now. I will direct the attention of the management to this matter.

I was discussing this vote the other night when the house rose at eleven o'clock, and I then pointed out that we as shareholders were dealing with the most important business in a financial way which parliament has to consider. I intended to point out the similarity between the corporate structure of the Canadian National Railway system and that of any other railway company, the only distinction being that in this instance we represent the great body of shareholders, the people of Canada, instead of those who have share certificates representing their interest in an enterprise. I had also pointed out that this was not a supply bill in the proper use of the word "supply", that it should not be included in the estimates of the government of Canada but should be a separate measure Just as the amount voted to the federal commission in Ottawa was a
(Mr. Dunning.]
separate measure, and just as the amounts voted to the harbour commissions of Halifax, St. John and Quebec were separate bills. I still think that is so.
We are asked to-night to vote some $39,000,000 to this railway system, and a very considerable part of that amount will be required to take care of obligations which already have been partly incurred. That is abundantly clear. We are now meeting the obligations of this railway system in two ways: For some years we made direct advances out of the treasury, advances of $7,000,000, $10,000,000, and $15,000,000 out of our revenues. We taxed the people of the country for this money, which was put in the general consolidated revenue fund and then paid out to this railway company. Then we adopted another course, that of guaranteeing security and enabling the railway company to borrow the money themselves. There was still another method adopted at one time, by which we issued our own securities, received the money and handed it over to the railway company This is the second time this year we have been called upon to vote money for this enterprise, the first item was in the supplementary estimates with respect to 1928, when we appropriated certain sums of money to make good the requirements of the undertaking. Now we are called upon to vote the very large sum of $39,00,000.
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which is the great competitor of this system, asks its shareholders for additional money by placing before them in the annual report which is presented to them, and which they receive before the meeting, a complete statement showing just for what the money will be required. I submit that parliament should have before it in the statute in detail the very same information given the shareholders of a privately owned enterprise in connection with its requirements. For instance, on page 8 of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company report for this year will be found the ten requirements in connection with branch lines. If you then turn over further you will find that the shareholders are asked to ratify and confirm certain leases and agreements which have been made. In another section you will find a request for the issue of additional common stock for the completion of hotels and generally for issuing new securities for the purpose of carrying on their undertaking. That is the way the matter is dealt with there. In this vote of $39,000,000 which will be placed upon the statutes of Canada there is not a single word to indicate where thi3 money is to be spent. When the shareholders

Supply-Railways-C.N.R. Hotels
of this company read the statutes of Canada and see this appropriation of $39,000,000 they will find it impossible to ascertain where that money is to be spent, the purposes for which it is to be used being stated only generally. The shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway receive this report; they know they are asked to vote money to the company, or are asked to enable the company to issue securities for the purpose of building branch lines, for the purpose of building new steamships and for the purpose of building new hotels. They are told where this money is to be spent; they are told the length of the proposed branch lines and are given an estimate of what they will cost. In some instances the 'directors indicate that they have made commitments, which they ask the shareholders to approve.
That is the position, Mr. Chairman, and why should we conduct this great enterprise of ours in this way, by putting before parliament in the very late days of the session without an adequate opportunity for discussion-that is perfectly clear-the statement that we require $39,000,000, indicating that the money may be obtained in any one of several ways and handed over to the management for the purpose of enabling them to meet the commitments of the undertaking? I submit that we have a right to know these things, just as in a statute providing money for a harbour commission we know that $500,000 is to be spent in Halifax harbour this year, with 'the purpose indicated for which it is to be used. When we pass statutes providing money for the harbours of Quebec or St. John we indicate very clearly for what that money is to be used, but look at this estimate which is placed before us. Will any member of this house, looking at that, estimate, be able to say with any degree of certainty where this money is to be used? All the fine print contained in the estimate is an indication of how the money may be raised, but where is this money to be used other than in connection with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine? Where is it to be used? I submit that we should know that with great particularity, as trustee shareholders representing the real shareholders, the people of Canada, so that when they pick up the statutes they may know that their trustees in this parliament voted certain sums of money on the recommendation of the management of this road, to be used in certain specific places.
We have been told that one of the uses to which part of this money is to be put is the construction of a hotel at Halifax. Where 56103-2541
do I find it in this vote? It is quite true that it was before a special committee and certain observations were made with respect to it, but that is not what the shareholders of the road have before them. What the shareholders of the road have before them are these estimates, and there is nothing there to indicate that a sum of money is to be used for the construction of a hotel at Halifax or elsewhere. I have the Canadian Pacific Railway report and I find reference made to what they have been doing with regard to the Banff Springs hotel, and I find reference made to expenditures they are making in other places with respect to hotel construction. The shareholders are asked to approve those expenditures.
I hope to make this point clear without taking more time in which to' develop it, but it seems to me that the management of the road should be so specific in the statement of their requirements for money, that they should ask us as trustee shareholders to appropriate this money, not in the estimates, but in a public bill, or an appropriation bill, call it what you like, rather than by supply estimates. We would then be able to look up the statutes and find the points at which the money was to be expended and discover to what extent this money had been used for the purpose for which it w.as earmarked.
I will not dwell to-night on the question of the finances of the road, although in my judgment these matters should be dealt with. There is growing up in this country the habit and custom on the part of some of the members to believe that because one offers a suggestion with respect to the condition of the Canadian National Railways he is reflecting upon the government of the day. That is not so. The government has some responsibility with respect to it, but any criticism is criticism against the government of the day only to the extent to which they permit conditions to continue which place a heavier and heavier obligation upon the people of this country. I wonder if the members of this house realize that we have permitted this undertaking, during the last year or two, so to increase its obligations that the burden of interest that must be met by this road has increased according to the last report, over a million dollars. A million dollars of additional interest to be earned is a very heavy charge upon the undertaking, having regard to the margin that exists between the gross and net earnings.
As I say, I will not dwell to-night upon the financial return. All you have to do is to see that during the year 1926 the road earned a little more than $2,000,000 over and above the amount necessary to pay the interest upon

By success I mean going there as members of this house with our criticisms and with our questions, particularly as relates to the major matters of the conduct of the country's business. We should do this in the manner in which the hon. member for Toronto-Sear-borough (Mr. Harris) went into the accounting. Perhaps he had an advantage, being a member of the committee, but, as I said before, this committee' has never yet denied to any member of this house the privilege of asking questions of the officers of the company. I would plead, therefore, in order that there might be a little more intelligent discussion of Canadian National affairs in the future in this house, that we make wider use as members of this house of that committee for the purpose of eliciting information, which once printed becomes easily available to all the people of Canada through the medium of the reports of the committee.

I do not intend to take
very much time, but my hon. friend has seen fit to make some references to myself; references which have arisen out of wrong information given to my hon. friend, or else he is endeavouring to place a construction on my actions in connection with this project which is entirely unwarranted.
As far back as 1913 a report was made to the government of which my hon. friend was a supporter at that time, regarding the port development at Halifax, as follows "that for the transatlantic trade as well as for the local and tourist trades hotel accommodation of the highest class adjoining the terminals will be a necessity." I want to remind my hon. friend that in 1926 two different gentlemen appeared before the commission presided over by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan. Mr. Cornell for the Halifax Board of Trade made his representations, and closed his remarks with this:
We hope that is the beginning of a move to appreciate the position at this end of the line and that the program of hotel accommodation 
will be extended to the city of Halifax, the city of Halifax being the chief port, and the chief Atlantic Canadian terminal of the railway.
He was speaking of the Canadian National Railways providing hotels in various places and soliciting tourist traffic. This was followed by the testimony of Hon. J. A. Walker, Minister of Natural Resources for Nova Scotia, who said:
It is highly desirable that the federal government should take immediate steps to establish a national park in the province, and the Canadian National Railways erect a first class hotel in Halifax, the capital, or main centre of the province.
The reference made in the Duncan report to this project is shown on page 43. This report states that a suggestion was made that there should be a hotel built by the Canadian National Railways at Halifax, and then goes on to say:
We feel it is not a subject matter upon whieh^ we can make any recommendation, as in our view it is a question for the judgment of the railway administration itself in the light of ordinary business considerations.
We have to-night -the recommendation made to the hon. Minister of Railways, the president of the road, every vice president of the road and the board of directors for a Canadian National hotel at Halifax. The matter has been referred to the special committee of this bouse and investigated by them, or if it was not- investigated it should have been, because the gentlemen who are sitting around my hon. friend were on that committee at the time. After investigation, it was recommended to the house.

How does the hon. minister justify another hotel in Halifax when the return issued to parliament last year showed that every one :of the ten Canadian National hotels were going behind in- the fixed charges?

I am not in the hotel business, but I am simply quoting authority which 'it seems to me ought to have some weight with this parliament and with this country. Hon. J. A. Walker, who was a member of the Conservative government in Halifax, justified it, as my hon. friend puts it.
A sort of political hotel.

Everyone who has inquired into this has recommended and has justified St. The special committee of this house has justified it. I do not propose to go into the matter in detail regarding the merits of an hotel at Halifax, but I might point out some

Supply-Railways-C.N.R. Hotels
very strong reasons why the Canadian National Railways should have a hotel there. The Canadian National Railways, enjoying as it does three-quarters of the traffic of the province of Nova Scoitia; having steamship connections at Halifax, Halifax being the beginning of ithe long haul across the continent, needs hotel accommodation there. If they did not have it people would go to other hotels and they would lose the opportunity of getting that long haul traffic. The Canadian National Steamships are developing a service to the West Indies which will have its terminal at Halifax. Business is constantly increasing through the port of Yarmouth, through a new line of steamers being put on from both New York and from Boston to Yarmouth, with the expectation of something like 40,000 tourists through Yarmouth this year, and the Canadian National Railways will expect to get a proportion of that traffic if they have a good hotel at Halifax. Not only the Canadian National Railways but other roads have seen the advantages of having hotel accommodation in order that they may have a better opportunity to route passengers over their lines-The Canadian Pacific has had the experience at Quebec, and I have no doubt the Canadian National have had the same experience at other points, that having a hotel at these points is a great advantage in getting a large number of travellers routed along their lines.
But I am not discussing the merits so much as I am the remarks which were made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. What he said with regard to somebody going to Yarmouth indicates how little he really knows of the situation. He mentioned a proposition that had been put up whereby the Canadian National Railways were to invest a quarter of a million dollars in a hotel proposition in Halifax, and he said some friends came to Yarmouth and intimated that it was these friends who influenced me against the hotel. I want to tell him that the friends who came to Yarmouth were Mr. W. H. Dennis, the manager of the Halifax Herald, the opposition paper in Halifax; Mr. H. R. Silver, who is well known as a leading Conservative in Halifax and who has been I think the president of the Conservative organization; Mr. J. G. Farqu'har, and Mr. Bain. These are the gentlemen who came to place before me a proposition in which they thought I might be interested as a member of the government, to the effect that the Canadian National Railways should invest a quarter of a million dollars in the hotel project. I want to say
to my hon. friend that it was due to no persuasion of theirs that I took the position I did; that I went over the proposition with them from end to end, and that I found out what my hon. friend practically admitted when he spoke first to-night, namely, that to say the least the proposition was extremely expensive. When we have in raising $1,084,000 to pay $150,000 in shrinkage of securities on a proposition which is going to be supported by two railways which are taking a large block of the preferred stock, you have a proposition that, it seems to me', requires close examination. My hon. friend was quite right when he suggested that he did not wonder from that point of view that I did not agree to the proposition that was made.
The proposition which was made at that time was this, namely, that the cumulative preferred stock was to be sold to the underwriters at 85 and that the Canadian National railways was to pay par for that stock. In other words the Canadian National railway was to pay $37,500 into the pockets of the promoters of the company. I thought that was not good enough from the point of view of government financing if there was some other way out. I realized exactly what the Canadian National situation was; I realized that it was thought it might be impossible to get an appropriation for a Canadian National hotel and that this was the best alternative offered. But I told those gentlemen there at the time-and I did not mince matters with them-I criticized the proposition. I told Mr. Bain in effect: "I am against your making this money out of it. You can hardly expect the government of Canada to approve a proposition of this kind and pay this amount of money into your pocket. I am for a Canadian National hotel if that is possible". My hon. friend talks about selling bonds. Does the committee think there would be any great trouble in selling $600,000 worth of bonds in a concern into which about $1,084,000 cash was to be put altogether and in which the preferred stock behind the bonds was to be largely taken by the two great railway systems of Canada, who would be in effect the guarantors of the concern? Would the bondholders stand much chance of losing their money? They would be pretty sure that the railways, in order to save their investment, would have to take the proposition over and their bonds would be perfectly safe. But even those' bonds were to be sold to the underwriters, Messrs. Bain and Company, at a ten per cent discount. That is, they were going to get the bonds at ninety which they were to sell to the public

Supply-Railways-C.N.R. Hotels
at one hundred. I do not think I am very far wrong and I am in the judgment of the house and the country when I say that I felt if a better proposition could be made for the people of Canada, it should be made. I told Mr. Bain at that time that I was against his making that money and I told the gentlemen that I believed in a Canadian National hotel and that I was going to work for it. That was the answer I gave them at that time and they went home.
And they were not your friends?

There are people within the sound of my voice who know whether in a political sense they were friends of mine or not. They were Mr. W. H. Dennis and Mr. H. R. Silver. They were political opponents of the strongest kind. I gave those gentlemen that information at that time. I came to Ottawa and the government held a meeting on July 14th. This is the statement which was given out at that time:
That the federal government is not prepared to authorize the expenditure of public funds in the purchase of a minority interest in a hotel project at Halifax, was one of the decisions made at to-day's meeting of the cabinet. The statement was made after the meeting that, quite apart from the features of the scheme itself, the government considered that large capital expenditures of this kind should, in the first instance, be submitted to parliament.
Hon. J. L. Ralston. Minister of National Defence, when seen this evening, stated that he had made his position clear to the promoters of the project two or three weeks ago, namely, that he was for a Canadian National hotel, in preference to spending public money on underwriting charges, and having the direction and management of the institution subject to the control of outside parties.
When asked regarding the prospects, Hon. Mr. Ralston said that the matter had gone so far that he had no doubt in his mind that if the board of directors of the Canadian National railways recommended a project for a railway terminal hotel at Halifax the government Mould see that it was submitted to parliament next session. He also stated that he would do all possible to assist such an undertaking.
May I pause here to say that in connection with the matter of control the Canadian National was to be away in the minority? Both railways, as a matter of fact, in that scheme were to be in the minority and the majority of voting power was to be held by Mr. Bain and his clients to whom the stock was sold. As I have read to the committee, the statement I made after the meeting of government was that if the Canadian National railway directorate would recommend a Can-

adian National hotel, I felt the matter had gone so far I was certain in my own mind that the government would submit it to par-lilament. What happened then? The next was a statement-and this is what my hon. friend did not refer to-made by Sir Henry Thornton on July 20th, just five days after, as follows:
In connection with the possible participation by the Canadian National railivay in the construction of the proposed Lord Nelson hotel at Halifax, the following statement was given out to-day in Montreal by Sir Henry Thornton, president of the national system:
In view of the fact that any partial investment in the proposed hotel at Halifax would ' require the approval of parliament, which could not be obtained until the next session, and the preference indicated that the Canadian National should construct and entirely own a hotel at _ Halifax, which is in accordance with the original desire of the railway, an appropriate amount will be included in the annual railway budget to be submitted at the next session of parliament.
It should be observed that no time will be lost in the execution of this policy, as in any case even a partial investment in the hotel would require parliamentary sanction, and, therefore, could not be made until the next session of parliament.
Newspapers in Halifax came out at that time accusing me of having blocked a project for a hotel at Halifax but I did not see any hats thrown in the air or any headlines in at least one newspaper, although there was a statement by a member of the government that, if there was a project for a Canadian National hotel, he believed the government would submit it to parliament if the railway directors would recommend it, and when there was a statement by the president of the company to the effect that the board would so recommend it. But the people of Halifax began to get a clearer view of the situation and they realized why the Canadian National felt that they should have an hotel and that the financial proposals were pretty extravagant for a government project. In August I was in Halifax and this is the report of an interview which the president of the board of trade and two members of their committee had with me. I take this from the Halifax Herald of August 20, 1927:
Colonel Ralston referred the committee to a statement he made in Ottawa cn July 14. expressing himself in favour of the project and also to a statement made by Sir Henry Thornton to the effect that an amount sufficient for the construction of a Canadian National railway hotel in Halifax would be placed in the railway estimates for submission to parliament at the next, session.
The Nova Scotia minister said there was no change in the situation, that it could be taken

Supply-Railways-C.N.R. Hotels
as authoritative that the matter would be placed before parliament.
The board of trade committee reported that they were cordially received.
That looked, it seemed to me, as if Halifax ought to feel there was a fair chance for having an hotel there. My hon. friend has taken occasion to-night to say-and this is what he must refer to-that this was a piece of partisan politics. I want to say to my hon. friend that I am flattered by the suggestion that I, a humble and junior member of the government, having just finished my first session in this house, had such power in the country that I was able to induce not only the government but Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors to recommend a thing which for the purpose of his argument he must assume they were against, a thing which was unwise, which was not in the interest of the road, simply because I wanted it dons for political purposes. My hon. friend gives me great credit. I do not claim to have that power and further than, that he must go the full length and he must say that in addition to that I have been able to get all the vicepresidents and the board of directors of the road to recommend it, and Sir Henry Thornton to come here and testify before this committee and to make the report which the minister has read to-night, all because of the fact that he was carrying out my political ideas. Simply to make that statement is a sufficient answer, I think. It is about as preposterous a thing as could be said; it is about as untrue a thing as could be said, and I want to tell my hon. friend that there is absolutely no foundation for it whatever. I have supported the Canadian National hotel project because I believed it was sound from the point of view of the people of Canada, and from the point of view of the people of Nova Scotia.
I want to mention one other thing. This hesitancy which I showed about accepting this project had another effect. I had pointed out to the gentlemen at Yarmouth that this proposition was a pretty expensive bit of financing. One of the gentlemen came to Ottawa just about the time the Government was meeting, and I pointed out to him agaih that this was an extremely expensive bit of financing, with the result that I have under my hand at the present time, if hon. members will believe me, a letter from him in which he advises me that in order to meet my views about the expensiveness of the proposition, Bain and Company will agree, if the government will put this through, to hand back $25,000 of the $37,500 which they were going to make out
of the Canadian National subscription. I think that was some accomplishment, and indicated some justification for the position I took. Later they presented another financial proposition, which reduced the $156,000 that was going to be made to $94,000, so that the company on the second scheme was going to get altogether $1,146,000, and were going to pay $94,000 for it. Even that I thought was a pretty expensive piece of financing for the government to authorize, and I do not think I can be blamed for having hesitated about that, or that the government can be blamed for taking the position which they did. They did not accept that proposition. As I have said, the statements by Sir Henry Thornton and myself were in July,'then came the interview with the board of trade representative. That interview was in August.
Then later in September and I do not blame them for it-it was legitimate competition- along came Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific railway and said-I do not think I am misreading his mind-" Here is an opportunity perhaps to cultivate the goodwill of the province of Nova Scotia. We will put up the whole $350,000 towards building the hotel." Mr. Beatty in a statement that appeared in newspapers not long ago made no reference to the facts which I have just related to the committee, namely, that it had been intimated in the statements by Sir Henry Thornton and myself in July that an estimate for a Canadian National hotel in Halifax would be submitted to Parliament. Mr. Beatty proposed, and his proposal was met with acclaim in Halifax at the time, to put up the $350,000 and to take the place of the Canadian National saying that he would give the Canadian National their stock if they desired it afterwards. Immediately, possibly the next day or the same day, Sir Henry Thornton came out with a reiteration of the statement he had previously made that he was for a Canadian National hotel, and said that the Canadian National would go on with their hotel. I have the statement here; it is very short.

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I understood that we were to sit here to get through some estimates. It is perfectly obvious that we are not going to get very far with the estimates to-night. Why not conclude this debate and adjourn?

Perhaps my hon. friend will realize that what has been said has been rather important from my point of view, and I think I should be allowed to say a word or two to see it through.

I shall not trouble the
house with reading the quotation. As I said, Sir Henry Thornton came out immediately with a further statement to the effect that the Canadian National would erect its own hotel in Halifax, and that has been his attitude. I do not want to take the time of the committee to read extracts, but I could read at least three different statements made in the public press of the country, by Sir Henry Thornton to the effect, as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has said, that the partial subscription in a hotel was altogether an alternative if they could not get the money for a Canadian National hotel.
I want the house and the committee to understand the situation. I want the people of Nova Scotia to understand the situation. My stand has been, first-, last and all the time, for a Canadian National hotel, and it has been so because I believe it was. in the interest of the country that if public funds are put into a hotel it should be a Canadian National hotel. After the Beatty hotel was announced, I made no further statement about it until Sir Henry Thornton represented that he believed that it was absolutely essential in the interests of the road, and as the Minister of Railways says that he considered that it was absolutely necessary in view of his competitive position in the province of Nova Scotia. I am for giving a fair chance to the people's road; and I do realize this fact, that the Canadian National has an interest in the province of Nova Scotia which it should be allowed to protect, I am only too glad to welcome the Canadian Pacific railway with their hotel and the statement I made to the

newspapers I stand by, namely, that I think it is a good thing for the province of Nova Scotia to see two big railway systems like the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific investing money in that province, because it will ensure their very active interest and give an impetus to trade and an increase to traffic all over the province. I do expect to see a great incentive to the tourist traffic and a great addition to activities in the various towns and villages throughout the province when we have these two hotels in Halifax.
I have taken more of the time of the committee than I intended. I believe that my stand will be justified in the future, and I am willing at any time to submit the records to this committee or to this country in order to vindicate the soundness of the position which I have taken.

I am not going to delay
the house very long, but I want to make this criticism.
I rise to a point of order. The Prime Minister asked us to sit until 12.30. It is now after one, and we have not passed a single estimate.

As I was about to say, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to go on record as opposing any expenditure of public money in the province of Nova Scotia, but I must criticize the government's attitude with regard to this hotel expenditure because their announcement came too late. For years, as will be observed from the statement of the Minister of National Defence, the people of Halifax have been looking forward to increased modern hotel accommodation. In 1913 we had a program laid down to develop the terminal at Halifax. If the minister had disclosed his policy a year ago this discussion would not be taking place to-night, for it would have been accepted by everybody not only in Nova Scotia, but throughout the Dominion, it being realized that we were in need of a good, modern hotel. The Lord Nelson hotel promoters would have ceased their activities. But after the negotiations reported here to-night the promoters of that hotel announced that they would proceed. A few days afterwards the Canadian National Railways announced that they had decided to build an up-to-date hotel and station at Halifax at a cost of a million and a quarter dollars. To my mind for a combined station and hotel that sum is not sufficient. To-day the new hotel is almost completed, against the protests of the management of the existing hotels. In full page advertisements they declared that no further hotel accommodation was needed. Those people are all friendly to this government. The Minister of National Defence will not deny that the management of the two leading hotels in Halifax are friendly to his government, and that they protested most vigorously against the building of the Lord Nelson hotel, because they urged that there was already sufficient accommodation. Now, we had the announcement of the Lord Nelson hotel promoters that they would proceed with their building, and immediately following that came the announcement of the Canadian National Railways.

An announcement was
made by Sir Henry Thornton on July 20 of

After a considerable amount of the stock in the new hotel had been sub. scribed.

After large advertisements had been put in the newspapers advertising the stock, notwithstanding the fact that the promoters knew of the matter of the Canadian National hotel had not been approved by the government.

After the announcement by the promoters of the Lord Nelson hotel that they were going to proceed with their project, I ask was it good busines for this government or the railway management to announce to the people the building of a second additional hotel, especially after the vigorous protest on the part of the management of the existing hotels that there was no need for further accommodation?
And notwithstanding that protest, I advocated the Canadian National Railway hotel.

think of that hotel to-day?
I have made my statement.

I think it would be far better for the railway management to proceed with the building of a railway station to replace the temporary shed which was erected after the explosion in 1916. The people have been clamouring for this for several years. The government should also provide further docking facilities and port improvements; if they want to spend a little more money, let them build the bridge across Halifax harbour that the people have been asking for. It may be said that increased port accommodation is not needed, but let me point out that the shipping tonnage of the port of Halifax is greater than that of the port of Montreal. My authority is the secretary of the Halifax Board of Trade. He states that in 1927 the gross tonnage, not including coasting ships, of the port of Halifax was 13,167,839 tons.
From the report of the Montreal harbour commission I notice that our gross tonnage was practically 500,000 more than it was the year before. Montreal is not open the year round but it is hailed as the great shipping port of Canada. The Minister of National Defence has mentioned the fact that there is increased steamship accommodation; larger steamers are being built to bring tourists into

Loan to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, repayable on demand with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council, upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine, and to be applied in payment of: deficits in operation of the company and of the vessels under the company's control during the year ending December 31, 1928, and capital requirements, $758,000.

All told the cost of these boats, lying up, runs into the vicinity of $100,000 a year. The fleet contains some twenty vessels of
